summary: isRedosSafeSource's hand-rolled character-class skip uses PCRE semantics (`]` immediately after `[` or `[^` is a literal member), but V8 treats `[^]` as a complete class meaning "any character". For a source containing `[^]`, the screen scans forward looking for a closing `]` that is not there, runs off the end of the string, and returns `budget = 1` — i.e. it never sees ANY of the source after `[^]`. Every hostile shape the screen exists to reject can be smuggled behind a three-character prefix.
failure: Reproduced on this tree. `isRedosSafeSource('[^](x+)+y')` returns **true**; `parseConfig({identity:{handle:'h'},topics:['t'],post_topics:['[^](x+)+y']})` is **accepted**; then `new Allowlist(['t'],{postPatterns:['[^](x+)+y']}).has('z' + 'x'.repeat(40))` — a 41-character topic, well under the 64-char MAX_MATCH_INPUT clamp — **blocked the event loop for 133,217 ms** before returning false. The clamp does not help: 41 chars is already far past the exponential knee, and 63 chars never returns. Blast radius is not limited to operator config: `engine/presence.ts:297` (`compilePeerPatterns`) applies the identical screen to `postTopics` sources carried in an UNTRUSTED peer presence beat, so one hostile beat wedges the single-threaded bridge on every `parley_list_users` call — permanently, since the beat is replayed from the presence topic on each roster build. The screen's own test header claims "whatever it accepts must MATCH in bounded time, for every input a caller can reach it with"; this is a direct counterexample.
remediation: Fix the class parser to JS semantics: after `[` (and an optional `^`), do NOT treat a leading `]` as a literal member — an immediate `]` closes the class. Then handle the two JS-legal empty forms explicitly (`[]` matches nothing, `[^]` matches any char, so charge `[^]` like `.`). Belt-and-braces: if the scan reaches end-of-string while still inside a class, return `false` rather than `true` — an unterminated scan means the screen lost track of the grammar and must fail closed. The same fail-closed rule should cover any future parser divergence.
testUpgrade: Class = "the hand-rolled source scanner disagrees with V8's regex grammar, so structure hides from the screen" — not the `[^]` instance. In regex-safety.test.ts, make the CORPUS a cross product: for every hostile shape already listed, also generate `PREFIX + shape` for PREFIX in ['', '[^]', '[]', '[a]', '[\\]]', '[]]', '[^]]', '\\[', '(?<n>a)', '(?i:a)'] and assert `isRedosSafeSource` rejects each, plus keep the existing "an accepted source matches in bounded time" property over that widened corpus with the PER_MATCH_BUDGET_MS wall clock (which is what would actually have caught this). Add a differential property test: for each generated source, assert that stripping every character-class span the SCREEN thinks it saw leaves a string whose bracket structure matches what `new RegExp(src)` accepts — a generator over random class-ish fragments would have found `[^]` without anyone naming it. Existing too-narrow tests: regex-safety.test.ts CORPUS lines 46-48 contain `'[\\]]*x'` and `'[*+?{}()|]+'` but no `[^]`/`[]` row at all, and allowlist.test.ts/config.test.ts HOSTILE tables are fixed lists with no class prefix.

summary: `new RegExp(`^(?:${src})$`)` assumes `src` is balanced. An unbalanced source is uncompilable on its own but becomes a LEGAL regex once wrapped, re-associating the anchors into an unanchored alternation branch. The Allowlist constructor never compiles the bare source, so it does not throw — it silently mints an allow-everything post/fetch set. The AllowlistOptions JSDoc (lines 36-38) states the opposite: "Config validation rejects both classes first; the constructor throws if one reaches here — `SyntaxError` for an uncompilable source."
failure: Reproduced on this tree. `new RegExp('ops)|(.*')` throws SyntaxError (unmatched `)`), yet `new Allowlist(['ctx'], { postPatterns: ['ops)|(.*'] })` **does not throw**, and `allow.has('secret-topic')` returns **true** — the wrap became `/^(?:ops)|(.*)$/`, whose second branch is unanchored at the front and matches every string. `allow.patterns()` still reports `['ops)|(.*']`, so the tool description surfaced to the agent also understates the reach. `Allowlist` is public barrel API (index.ts:40) and index.test.ts pins it as kept surface, so an embedder building one by hand (or any composition root that does not route through parseConfig) gets a wide-open post/fetch allowlist from a config line that reads as narrow. The identical wrap with NO bare-compile check is used on genuinely untrusted input at engine/presence.ts:297-300 (`compilePeerPatterns`), where round 1 already filed it; it is still present. Only the parseConfig path is safe, and only incidentally, because config.ts:200 happens to compile the bare source first.
remediation: Move the balance check into the one place that owns the wrap: in the Allowlist constructor, compile `new RegExp(src)` bare BEFORE compiling the wrapped form, and let the SyntaxError propagate (or convert it to a named error). Better, assert the wrap is faithful — compile both and reject if the source is not a single balanced group-free-of-escapes unit; simplest sufficient check is that the bare source compiles. Apply the same in `compilePeerPatterns` (skip the source there, since peer input is untrusted). Then either delete or correct the AllowlistOptions JSDoc claim.
testUpgrade: Class = "a source is validated in one form and compiled in another, so the wrap changes its meaning". Parameterized case over wrap-escaping sources — ['ops)|(.*', 'a)|(.*', 'a)(b', 'x)$|^(', '(a', 'a|', ')('] — asserted at BOTH ends: (1) `new Allowlist(['ctx'], {postPatterns:[src]})` throws, and (2) if any such construction is ever allowed, `has(<random topic not matched by the source's intent>)` is false. Add a property test that generates a random source, and asserts `Allowlist.has(t)` agrees with `new RegExp('^(?:'+src+')$').test(t)` ONLY when `new RegExp(src)` also compiles — otherwise the constructor must have thrown. Mirror the identical table into presence.test.ts for `compilePeerPatterns`/`filterReachable`. Existing too-narrow tests: allowlist.test.ts 'Allowlist post patterns' only ever feeds 'ctx-.*' and 'exp/[a-z]+'; config.test.ts:85 covers 'ctx-(' but only on the parseConfig path, which is the one path that is already safe.

summary: `isNoSuchTopicError` was written, exported, barrel-pinned and given 14 tests specifically because `instanceof` answers "was this thrown by MY class object", not "is this the seam contract" — yet NOT ONE recognition site in core uses it. The exact failure its own JSDoc names ("every `instanceof` check in core then reads a plugin's 'topic does not exist yet' as a hard backend failure") is fully present, while the helper's isolated test suite makes the class look guarded.
failure: Traced through every call site (grep over packages/bridge-core/src and packages/*/src: the only non-export reference to `isNoSuchTopicError` anywhere in the monorepo is its own test). Failing setup: a consumer pins `@sharptrick/parley-core@A` at the root while `@sharptrick/parley-discord` (or `-slack`) resolves a nested `@sharptrick/parley-core@B` — npm's normal behaviour on a version conflict, and both plugins genuinely throw `NoSuchTopicError` (bridge-discord/src/index.ts:383, bridge-slack/src/index.ts:95). `parley_fetch_recent` on a Discord channel id that does not exist → the plugin throws its copy's class → tools.ts:218 evaluates `e instanceof <root copy's class>` → **false** → the error propagates as a hard tool failure instead of the documented empty replayable page. Same input through `catchUpAll` on session start aborts catch-up for the whole topic list; same through `startPushLoop` throws and the bridge fails to attach its live path entirely — the one case push-loop.ts's own JSDoc promises is "skipped so the remaining topics still go live". No test anywhere constructs a foreign-copy NoSuchTopicError and drives it through catchup/tools/push-loop; the only foreign twins in the repo (`DuplicateInstall`, the vm-realm class) live in no-such-topic.test.ts and are never handed to a plugin fake.
remediation: Replace all five `instanceof NoSuchTopicError` sites with `isNoSuchTopicError(err)`. Also harden the helper itself: it compares against `NoSuchTopicError.name` (the derived `Function.name`) while the constructor assigns the string literal `'NoSuchTopicError'` — under any bundler that mangles class names those diverge, so compare against the literal that the constructor writes. Then add a lint/test guard that `instanceof NoSuchTopicError` appears nowhere outside no-such-topic.ts.
testUpgrade: Class = "a cross-realm/duplicate-install-safe predicate exists but the consuming code still uses the identity check it was meant to replace". Do not test the predicate in isolation. Parameterize the EXISTING foreign twins (native / duplicate-install / vm-realm / bare `{name:'NoSuchTopicError'}`) as a table, and run each one through every consumer path — `catchUpTopic`, `catchUpAll`, `startPushLoop`, `parley_fetch_recent`, `parley_list_users` — via a FakePlugin whose `fetchRecent`/`subscribe` rejects with that twin, asserting each path degrades to "topic absent" rather than throwing. That table is the ratchet: a sixth consumer added later fails it the moment it uses `instanceof`. Complement with a source-hygiene-style assertion that `/instanceof NoSuchTopicError/` matches only no-such-topic.ts, so the class cannot come back under a new call site.

summary: config.test.ts carries two impressive fixture walkers (unknown-key near-misses, empty-string leaves) that make config coverage look exhaustive, but there is not one assertion on any numeric bound. Verify the upgrade by re-running the mutation above and watching it go red.

summary: `fetchRecent`'s JSDoc documents a two-branch contract for an absent topic: empty page with a replayable `nextCursor`, OR `NoSuchTopicError`. The frozen shared suite in packages/conformance can only certify the first branch — its 'fetchRecent on a never-posted topic' case (index.ts:184) asserts `messages` is `[]` and would fail outright on a plugin that takes the documented second branch. Both plugins that actually use it opt out by pre-provisioning in `freshTopic`, so the branch is graded only by each plugin's private tests, in each plugin's own shape.
failure: Traced. packages/conformance/src/index.ts:184-191 calls `ctx.plugin.fetchRecent({topic: ctx.freshTopic()})` and asserts `first.messages` equals `[]`; a plugin that throws `NoSuchTopicError` here — which seam.ts:120 explicitly says it MAY do — fails conformance. bridge-discord/test/conformance.test.ts:32-35 sidesteps this by having `freshTopic()` call `fake.createChannel(id)` first, with a comment routing the absent-topic case to rest-contract.test.ts; bridge-slack does the same in absent-topic.test.ts. Consequence: the shared suite — the artefact CLAUDE.md names as the proof that adding a backend needs no core change — cannot tell a plugin that throws `NoSuchTopicError` on genuinely-absent topics from one that throws a plain `Error` (which core must propagate as a hard failure) or one that invents a cursor. A new backend implementing the documented second branch has no shared case telling it which errors are which.
remediation: Give the conformance context an optional `absentTopic?: () => Topic` (a topic the backend genuinely cannot represent, distinct from `freshTopic`), and make the never-posted case accept EITHER documented branch explicitly: empty page with replayable cursor, or a rejection for which `isNoSuchTopicError` is true. Add a companion case asserting that a NON-absence failure from the same call is NOT recognised as absence, so the discrimination — not just the happy path — is what is certified.
testUpgrade: Class = "a seam contract with two legal branches where the shared suite only grades one, pushing the other into per-plugin tests that cannot agree". Parameterize the absent-topic case over both branches in packages/conformance and require every backend to declare which one it takes (a context field, so silence is a failure rather than a skip). Widen it with the foreign-copy error twins from finding 3 so the branch is graded through `isNoSuchTopicError`, not `instanceof`. Existing too-narrow tests: bridge-discord/test/rest-contract.test.ts and bridge-slack/test/absent-topic.test.ts each pin the branch in one vendor's error vocabulary and neither is reachable from the shared suite.

summary: `buildMessage` is documented as "the single sanctioned way to assemble a normalized Message from a backend record" and is the one choke point every plugin passes through, yet it validates nothing. An empty `id` or an empty `cursor` — the two fields the whole dedup/ordering contract rests on — pass straight through and produce a Message that violates the contract the conformance suite pins, with the failure surfacing far from its cause.
failure: Traced. `buildMessage({topic: asTopic('t'), sender: 'a', content: 'x', timestamp: 'not-a-date', id: ''})` returns `{backendMsgId: '', cursor: '', timestamp: 'not-a-date', ...}` without complaint. `cursor: asCursor(input.cursor ?? input.id)` uses `??`, so an explicitly-passed empty-string cursor does NOT fall back to `id` either — a plugin that computes `cursor` and gets `''` silently ships an empty order key. Downstream, an empty cursor is persisted as read-state and replayed as `since`, where every falsy-check in the pipeline reads it as "no cursor" and re-fetches the backend's default window; an empty `backendMsgId` collapses the SeenSet dedup namespace so the first message of a topic suppresses all subsequent ones. packages/conformance/src/index.ts:60-63 asserts `backendMsgId.length > 0`, `cursor.length > 0` and `Date.parse(timestamp)` is not NaN — i.e. the project already treats these as contract, but enforces them only in the suite, not at the constructor every plugin actually calls.
remediation: Make `buildMessage` fail fast on the three invariants the suite already asserts: non-empty `id`, non-empty resolved `cursor` (and treat `''` as absent so it falls back to `id`), and a `timestamp` that parses. Throw a named error identifying the offending field and topic, so a plugin bug surfaces at the record it came from rather than three layers later in read-state or dedup.
testUpgrade: Class = "the single sanctioned constructor for a contract type does not enforce the contract, so violations surface far from their source". Parameterized table in message.test.ts over degenerate inputs — `id: ''`, `cursor: ''`, `cursor: '   '`, `timestamp: ''`, `timestamp: 'not-a-date'`, `sender: ''` — asserting `buildMessage` throws and names the field. summary: The per-request teardown fires `void transport.close()` and `void server.close()` with no `.catch`, so a rejecting close escapes as an unhandledRejection and terminates the remote-mode process.
failure: Stub `StreamableHTTPServerTransport.prototype.close` to reject (a real transport can reject on a socket already destroyed), POST one `initialize` to `/mcp`. Reproduced: two `unhandledRejection` events fire ~1 tick after the response closes; under Node's default `--unhandled-rejections=throw` the whole remote server dies on a single malformed/aborted request. Every other fire-and-forget site in the package (`emitChannel` in push-loop.ts:39, every presence beat) does attach a catch — this one alone does not, and `unhandled-rejection.test.ts` tables only those two sites, so the HTTP path is uncovered.
remediation: Attach a swallow-and-log handler: `void transport.close().catch((e) => console.error('[parley] transport close failed:', e))` and likewise for `server.close()`; or `void Promise.allSettled([transport.close(), server.close()])`.
testUpgrade: Widen `unhandled-rejection.test.ts`'s existing `FAILURE_SHAPES` table to a THIRD axis: enumerate every fire-and-forget call site in engine/+transport/ (presence beat, push emit, HTTP per-request transport.close, HTTP per-request server.close, presence stop on http close) × every failure shape, asserting `escaped === []`. Add a static guard test that greps the package source for `void <expr>(` not followed by `.catch(` — the class is 'a voided promise with no catch', not this one call.

summary: `RemoteHttpServer.close()` calls `httpServer.close()` unconditionally, so it rejects with ERR_SERVER_NOT_RUNNING after a failed `listen()` and on any second `close()`.
failure: `const s = createRemoteHttpApp(...); await s.listen(takenPort).catch(()=>{}); await s.close()` → rejects `Error: Server is not running.` (reproduced). Same for `await s.listen(0); await s.close(); await s.close()`. A composition root doing `try { await app.listen(p) } finally { await app.close() }` — or a SIGINT handler racing an explicit shutdown — surfaces a spurious fatal. The two existing bind-failure tests (http.test.ts:110, :126) hide it precisely because their cleanup is `await app.close().catch(() => {})`.
remediation: Guard the close: `if (httpServer === undefined || httpServer.listening !== true) { httpServer = undefined; resolve(); return; }`, and clear `httpServer` after a successful close so the object is re-listenable and close-idempotent.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a lifecycle table over the ORDER of `listen`/`close` calls — `[close], [listen-fail, close], [listen, close, close], [listen, close, listen, close], [listen-fail, listen-ok, close]` — asserting each terminal `close()` RESOLVES and no presence loop survives it. Ban bare `.catch(() => {})` in these tests' cleanup: the swallow is what let this ship.

summary: A cancelled long-poll that never got a page back throws a synthetic Error instead of returning, and that branch has no test at all.
failure: `parley_fetch_recent({ topic: 't', block_ms: 30000 })` with no `since` (the tool explicitly invites this: 'Omit for the recent window'); the client cancels, or the HTTP response closes, before the first `fetchRecent` settles. `untilAborted` yields ABORTED, `abandoned(undefined)` throws `fetch_recent cancelled before any page was read`, which propagates out of the handler and is rendered as a tool ERROR — a routine cancellation reported as a failure. Every row of the otherwise-thorough abort table (blocking-fetch.test.ts:151-206, :236-296) passes `since: tail`, so the `since === undefined` column is never entered.
remediation: Either return the first page's cursor once one exists and, before that, resolve with the plugin's own `nextCursor` from a final non-blocking probe; or (simplest, and consistent with 'core never mints cursors') throw a distinguishable `AbortError` (`name: 'AbortError'`) that the tool handler maps to a normal empty result rather than an isError.
testUpgrade: Make `since` a dimension of the existing abort table rather than a constant: {no since, since at tail} × {ignores blockMs, honours blockMs} × {abort before first fetch, during flight, during nap}. Assert every cell returns (or rejects with a recognisable AbortError) within the bound — the added column is the whole finding.

summary: `parley_fetch_recent`'s `limit` is accepted as any positive integer and passed straight to the plugin, while the neighbouring `block_ms` is clamped server-side to `catchup.block_max_ms`.
failure: A prompt-injected agent (the stated threat model — inbound message content becomes agent context) calls `parley_fetch_recent({ topic: 'ctx', limit: 100000000 })`. Core does not clamp it: the value reaches `plugin.fetchRecent` verbatim, then core iterates the whole result twice (JSON.stringify for the tool result, and `markSeen` over every id, which also flushes the 4096-entry FIFO and can un-dedup genuinely live messages). Nothing in the config surface caps it; `catchup.limit` (default 100) governs only the startup driver. Traced through tools.ts:200-224; no cap exists on any path.
remediation: Add a `catchup.fetch_max_limit` (default e.g. 1000) and clamp exactly as `block_ms` is clamped: `limit: Math.min(limit ?? default, deps.fetchMaxLimit)`. Fail-soft (clamp) rather than reject, matching the existing `block_ms` precedent.
testUpgrade: A single 'every numeric tool argument is bounded server-side' table enumerating each numeric field across all four tools (`limit`, `block_ms`, `since_ms`, list_users `limit`) × {0-adjacent, default, 10x the cap, Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER}, asserting the value the plugin/roster layer actually receives is <= the documented cap. That guards the class as new tools and fields are added.

summary: `parley_list_users` is covered by ~25 flat `it()`s whose setups are near-copies differing in one presence beat or one option, so no dimension can be seen — or independently fail — as a dimension.

Keep the three genuinely distinct behavioural cases (untrusted-pattern ReDoS bounds, NoSuchTopicError vs generic failure, presence-topic isolation) as their own named tests.

summary: No terminal Express error handler is installed and `env` is never pinned to production, so every OAuth/consent route falls through to Express's DEVELOPMENT default handler, which renders `err.stack` into the HTTP response. The /mcp handler in transport/http.ts is careful about this ("Never echo internal error detail to the client") — the browser-facing front door is not.
failure:
Unauthenticated `POST /parley/consent` with `content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` and a 200 KB body (over body-parser's 100 KB default) returns HTTP 413 whose HTML body is `
PayloadTooLargeError: request entity too large
    at readStream (/tmp/careening/worktrees/core-auth/node_modules/raw-body/index.js:163:17)
    at ...` — full stack plus absolute install paths. Reproduced against a live createOAuthRemoteApp with NODE_ENV unset, which is exactly what examples/self-host-remote/README.md's run command produces (it sets PARLEY_ISSUER_URL/PARLEY_TRUST_PROXY/PORT/HOST and nothing else). The same fallback covers /token, /register, /revoke and /authorize.
remediation: Mount a terminal error handler in createRemoteHttpApp (after configureApp and the /mcp routes) that logs the error server-side and responds with a status-only generic body, and set `app.set('env','production')` so Express can never choose the stack-rendering branch regardless of how the operator launches the process.
testUpgrade: Parameterize over EVERY route the app mounts (/mcp, /authorize, /token, /register, /revoke, /parley/consent) x every generic failure trigger (oversize body, malformed body for the route's content-type, unsupported media type) x NODE_ENV in {unset,'development','production'}, asserting the response body contains none of `node_modules`, `at ` frames, or the process cwd. That widened generator also catches any future hand-mounted route. The existing consent tests only drive the happy and ConsentError paths, so no current row ever reaches Express's fallback.

summary: `auth.oidc.jwks_uri` — the location of the keys every delegated-mode token is verified against — is validated only as `z.string().url()`, with no https requirement and, by construction, no origin check (it is the documented "trusted pin" that bypasses the issuer-origin check). The `issuer` field beside it IS https-gated, with the rationale "the JWKS trust root depends on TLS". The rationale is applied to the wrong field.
failure: `createOidcRemoteApp(plugin, cfg, { publicUrl, oidc: { issuer: 'https://kc.corp.example/realms/parley', allowed_subjects: ['s'], jwks_uri: 'http://jwks.attacker-reachable.example/keys' } })` boots clean, and `parseConfig` accepts the identical YAML. jose then fetches the verification keys over plaintext HTTP from a foreign origin; anyone on that path serves their own JWKS and forges a token that passes every gate (iss/aud/exp/sub are all attacker-chosen at that point). Reproduced. Contrast: the same config with `issuer: 'http://kc.corp.example/...'` is refused by both the schema and the SDK's checkIssuerUrl.
remediation: Apply the same predicate to `jwks_uri` in OidcAuthSchema and re-assert it in invariants.ts (which exists precisely because the schema is bypassable by the public factory): https, or an explicit loopback host. Reword the config comment so the stated reason attaches to the field it actually protects.
testUpgrade: A table over every config field that names a network trust root — `issuer`, `jwks_uri`, and any future endpoint override — crossed with {https non-loopback: boots, http loopback: boots, http non-loopback: refused}, run through BOTH parseConfig and the public factory. Ratchets the class "a URL the auth layer will fetch keys or metadata from must satisfy the transport invariant no matter which knob supplied it". invariants.test.ts currently runs this shape for publicUrl only.

summary: The RFC 8707 resource id is `new URL(mcpPath, publicUrl)`. invariants.ts guards publicUrl against every component that could relocate or corrupt that identifier, but mcpPath — the other operand of the same expression, and a public option on all three factories — is never validated at all.
failure: `createOAuthRemoteApp(plugin, cfg, { issuerUrl: new URL('http://127.0.0.1:PORT'), verifyOwner, mcpPath: '//evil.example/mcp' })` yields `app.resource.href === 'http://evil.example/mcp'` (reproduced). PRM then advertises a resource on a foreign origin, every token is minted with that audience, and `app.post('//evil.example/mcp')` never matches a real request, so the endpoint the owner just consented to is a permanent 404. `mcpPath: '/mcp/'` similarly produces a trailing-slash resource id, directly contradicting the `// canonical resource id (no trailing slash)` comment on the same line, and every NEAR_MISS_RESOURCES row proves a trailing slash is treated as a different resource.
remediation: Add `assertMcpPath(mcpPath)` to invariants.ts, called by both factories: require a leading single slash, no authority (`//`), no scheme, no query/fragment, and no trailing slash — and assert the derived resource's origin still equals publicUrl's origin before anything is advertised.
testUpgrade: Extend the existing BASE_URL_SHAPES matrix in invariants.test.ts into a two-dimensional one (base URL shape x mcpPath shape), with mcpPath rows for '/mcp', 'mcp', '/mcp/', '//evil.example/mcp', 'https://evil.example/mcp', '/mcp?x=1', '/mcp#f', ''. Every booting row must state the exact resource href AND assert `resource.origin === publicUrl.origin`; every other row must be refused. Guards the class "the advertised resource id is a function of two inputs and both must be constrained".

summary: Nothing in the suite asserts anything about the credential `issue()` produces beyond truthiness. Two independent mutations to the minting path leave all 1026 bridge-core tests green.
failure: Mutation 1: `randomBytes(32)` -> `randomBytes(3)` for both the access and refresh token. Suite green. A 24-bit bearer token is exhaustively guessable against `verifyAccessToken` in seconds, and /mcp has no rate limiter of its own. Mutation 2: `exchangeAuthorizationCode` -> `this.issue(client.client_id, [...rec.scopes, 'admin'], ...)`. Suite green — the AS silently grants a scope the owner's consent page never displayed and the client never requested. The refresh path has an explicit "may narrow but never widen" table; the authorization-code path has no scope assertion anywhere.
remediation: Keep randomBytes(32), and assert the granted scope set equals the consented set at exchange time. Both are cheap to pin.
testUpgrade: One parameterized 'every credential this AS mints' table with a row per credential kind (authorization code, access token, refresh token) asserting (a) decoded length >= 32 bytes and >= 128 bits of measured distinctness across 1000 mints, and (b) `tokens.scope` split equals exactly the scopes carried on the consent page / the prior grant — driven through BOTH the code-exchange and refresh-rotation entry points, so a new grant type must add a row. Guards the class "the artefact's own properties, not just its acceptance, are the security contract".

summary: `// Consume before every remaining check, so that a failed exchange leaves nothing replayable.` and the test block titled "an authorization code is single-use on any failed exchange" both claim a universal. The most security-relevant failure — a PKCE mismatch — does not consume the code, because the SDK runs that check between `challengeForAuthorizationCode` (which deliberately does not delete, per the comment two methods above) and `exchangeAuthorizationCode`. The file therefore contains two comments that contradict each other, and the test's title covers a table of one.
failure: Reproduced over HTTP against createOAuthRemoteApp: mint a code via the full DCR/PKCE/consent flow, then `POST /token` with a random code_verifier -> 400 `{"error":"invalid_grant","error_description":"code_verifier does not match the challenge"}`; immediately replay the SAME code with the correct verifier -> 200 with a live access_token and refresh_token. Under the stated invariant the second call must be invalid_grant.
remediation: Make the invariant true rather than narrowing the prose: consume the code in `challengeForAuthorizationCode` and carry the challenge forward in a short-lived redemption record that `exchangeAuthorizationCode` consumes, or add an explicit failed-attempt counter that burns the code. If it is deliberately declined, delete the universal comment and rename the describe block — but adjudicate that in the commit message, not in the file.
testUpgrade: Turn the single redirect_uri row into a table over EVERY way a token exchange can fail — wrong redirect_uri, absent redirect_uri, foreign client_id, wrong code_verifier, unserved `resource` — each row asserting that a subsequent fully-correct exchange of the same code is refused. Drive it over HTTP so the SDK's interleaved PKCE step is inside the system under test; the current provider-level test cannot see that step at all.

summary: The background sweeper is the only thing bounding the provider's four in-memory maps in a long-running server, and nothing tests that it is armed or that it is unref'd. The sweep test calls the private `sweep()` directly; the timer test only spies `clearInterval` call count.
failure: Mutating the constructor to `setInterval(() => undefined, SWEEP_INTERVAL_MS)` and deleting `this.sweepTimer.unref?.()` leaves all 1026 bridge-core tests green (verified). In that state the pending/codes/access/refresh maps grow without bound for the life of the process — `pending` is the one an unauthenticated caller can grow — and an un-stopped provider pins the event loop open, which is exactly what the `// Keep the .unref(), so that ...` comment warns against.
remediation: No production change needed; the code is correct today. Close the coverage hole so it stays correct.
testUpgrade: A parameterized 'every background timer this module arms' case using vi.useFakeTimers: construct the provider, seed one artefact of each expiring kind, advance the fake clock past SWEEP_INTERVAL_MS + each TTL WITHOUT calling sweep(), and assert each map is empty; plus a row asserting `sweepTimer.hasRef() === false`. Extending teardown.test.ts's setInterval-handle recorder to also assert each created handle was unref'd covers the second half across every factory, so a newly added loop inherits it.

summary: All OAuth state — DCR registrations, authorization codes, access and refresh tokens, pending consents — lives in five in-process Maps with no persistence. Nothing in examples/self-host-remote/README.md, packages/bridge-core/README.md, docs/keycloak-integration.md or DESIGN.md says so (grepped: the only 'restart' hit in the docs is DESIGN.md:222 about message history).
failure: A `systemctl restart parley` — or a crash, or a redeploy after the README's own "Refresh tools list" step — silently invalidates Claude's registration and both tokens; the owner must re-enter the passphrase with no error explaining why. Worse, an operator who scales the reverse-proxy target to two replicas gets a flow that fails ~50% of the time at /token with `invalid_grant`, because the code was minted in one process and redeemed in the other, and nothing anywhere warns against it.
remediation: State both constraints in examples/self-host-remote/README.md ("single process only; a restart requires re-consent") and in the ParleyOAuthProvider class doc, next to the existing single-tenant claim. This is the same class of deployment-shaping note the README already does well for PARLEY_TRUST_PROXY.
testUpgrade: Extend the docs-vs-code assertions already present in this package (hygiene.test.ts's barrel-coverage scan is the model) with a claims table: each row a documented remote-mode operational property and a predicate over the code — e.g. 'the deployment guide names every store that is process-local' asserted against the set of `new Map()` fields on ParleyOAuthProvider, so adding a sixth in-memory store forces the doc row. Guards the class "a deployment constraint that exists only in the implementation".

summary: connect() on an already-connected plugin silently replaces the driver, statements, storeId and prune timer without tearing down the previous ones — leaking the old driver and the old setInterval, and leaving every existing poll loop running against the new store with the old store's lastSeen. It also clears the health map, so subscriptionHealth() reports nothing wrong.
failure: Reproduced: `p.connect({db_path:a.db}); post x20; p.subscribe('ctx', h); p.connect({db_path:b.db}); p.post('ctx','new-1')` -> handler receives NOTHING (lastSeen=20 from a.db is above b.db's rowid 1), and `p.subscriptionHealth()` returns `[]` rather than reporting the dead loop. The first driver is never close()d (fd + WAL reader lock leak) and the first prune setInterval is never cleared, so it keeps firing hourly against the new store forever. The seam declares connect/disconnect as the lifecycle, so an embedder or any future core reconnect path hits silent, permanent loss of live push.
remediation: Make connect() fail fast when this.driver !== undefined (`throw new Error('SqlitePlugin already connected — call disconnect() first')`), or make it perform a full internal disconnect() (clear cancellers, clearInterval/clearTimeout, driver.close(), reset health) before opening the new store. A silent no-op-with-leak is the one option that must not remain.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized lifecycle table to test/background-jobs.test.ts covering the CLASS 'a lifecycle call in an unexpected order must fail loudly or fully re-establish, never half-apply': rows = [connect->connect, connect->subscribe->connect, connect->disconnect->connect, connect->disconnect->disconnect, subscribe-after-disconnect, post-after-disconnect], each asserting either a thrown error naming the plugin OR that (a) a message posted afterwards is delivered to a live handler, (b) subscriptionHealth() lists exactly the loops that can still deliver, and (c) no timer/driver from the previous generation survives (assert via a setInterval/setTimeout spy that every timer created in generation N is cleared). Existing tests never call connect() twice on one instance, so nothing here can fail today.

summary: BACKOFF_CEILING_MS — the constant that makes the README's 'backs off exponentially (to 30 s) and keeps probing' true, i.e. the guarantee that a topic whose DB was temporarily unreachable resumes live push within 30s rather than days — is asserted by no test. The whole suite is green with the ceiling effectively removed.
failure: Mutation: `const BACKOFF_CEILING_MS = 30_000_000_000;` (~347 days). `npx vitest run packages/bridge-sqlite/test/background-jobs.test.ts packages/bridge-sqlite/src/index.test.ts` -> 92/92 passed. The healable error-class cases only drive BURST=13 failures, so the computed delay is pollInterval*2^4 = 160ms and never reaches the cap; the persistent-failure cases only assert state==='degraded' and diags.length<=3. So a change that turns a 30-second recovery into a multi-day one ships green, and the README claim would be false with no test red.
remediation: Assert the ceiling through its consequence: with a small poll interval, drive failures well past ESCALATE_AFTER (e.g. 25+) so the uncapped delay would exceed the ceiling, then heal the statement and assert delivery resumes within a bound derived from BACKOFF_CEILING_MS (not from the raw exponent). Equivalently, export `backoffMs` and pin the sequence.
testUpgrade: Parameterize over the CLASS 'every latency/cost tunable that bounds recovery is pinned by an observable': a table of (failures, expectedDelayBound) rows for backoffMs — [10, 11, 15, 20, 40, 1000] — asserting monotonic non-decreasing delay AND delay <= BACKOFF_CEILING_MS for every row, plus one end-to-end case that breaks the poll statement for 30 consecutive ticks and then asserts a post is delivered within ~2*BACKOFF_CEILING_MS. Widen the same table to cover PRUNE_INTERVAL_MS and DIAG_INTERVAL_MS, which are equally unpinned today.

summary: disconnect() never touches this.health, so subscriptionHealth() keeps reporting state:'live' for every topic after the plugin has been torn down. The README markets this as the programmatic signal an embedder or health check reads, so it actively lies at exactly the moment live push is definitively down.
failure: Reproduced: `connect(); await subscribe('ctx', ()=>{}); await disconnect(); p.subscriptionHealth()` -> `[{"topic":"ctx","state":"live","consecutiveFailures":0}]`. A supervisor polling subscriptionHealth() to decide whether to restart the bridge sees a healthy live-push loop on a plugin whose driver is closed and whose timers are cancelled.
remediation: In disconnect(), mark every health entry `state: 'stopped'` (with a lastError such as 'disconnected') rather than leaving 'live' — 'stopped' already means 'will never deliver again without a reconnect', which is exactly true. Do not simply clear the map: an empty array is also read as 'nothing wrong'.
testUpgrade: Add a state-transition table to test/background-jobs.test.ts covering the CLASS 'subscriptionHealth() never claims a loop can deliver when it cannot': rows = [after subscribe -> live, after a healable burst -> degraded, after a fatal burst -> stopped, after disconnect -> stopped, after disconnect+reconnect -> absent-or-live], each asserting the reported state and then asserting the reality by posting and checking whether the handler fires. That reality cross-check is what stops the field from being a decorative string.

summary: MAX_PAGE (10000) is a hard rejection invented below the seam, but core's config schema validates `catchup.limit` as any positive integer. There is no way for a plugin to declare its maximum page size, so an operator config core certified as valid kills the bridge at startup, after connect() has already opened the store.
failure: Reproduced against the built CLI: a config with `catchup: { limit: 20000 }` loads cleanly (core's zod schema is `z.number().int().positive()`), connect() succeeds, then catch-up-on-start dies: `parley-sqlite: fatal: Error: parley-sqlite: invalid limit 20000 for topic ctx — expected an integer between 1 and 10000 ... at catchUpTopic (.../engine/catchup.js:33)`. The bridge never starts. The message names the plugin ceiling but never names the config key (`catchup.limit`) the operator has to change, and it arrives at catch-up time rather than at config load.
remediation: Surface this at the seam rather than absorbing it: add an optional declared page ceiling to BackendPlugin (e.g. `maxPageSize?: number`) that core clamps `catchup.limit` against at bridge build, failing fast with the config key named. As a plugin-local stopgap that does not change the seam, make normalizeLimit's message name `catchup.limit` / the `limit` tool argument as the thing to lower, so the error is actionable without reading plugin source.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized CLI/bridge-startup case covering the CLASS 'every operator-settable core config value that reaches a plugin is either validated where it is set or fails with the setting named': drive buildBridge/createStdioBridge over a table of core config values that plugins constrain — catchup.limit at [1, 100, MAX_PAGE, MAX_PAGE+1], catchup.block_max_ms, poll cadence — asserting either a clean start or a rejection whose message contains the YAML key path. Today no test drives core config through the sqlite plugin at all, which is why this passes unnoticed.

summary: The node:sqlite fallback is a documented, shipped mode ('falls back to Node's built-in node:sqlite ... the plugin code above the driver doesn't care which one is active') and no test ever runs a single line of it. Every test resolves better-sqlite3, and driver.test.ts explicitly `describe.skipIf(BetterCtor === null)`s the interesting blocks — a guard that in CI never fires, so the fallback is 0%-covered while the README states a parity guarantee.
failure: No input produces a wrong answer today — I forced the fallback (Module._load stub making better-sqlite3 look MODULE_NOT_FOUND) and drove openDriver + connect/post/fetchRecent/subscribe/pragma read-back/0600 at-rest mode: all pass, driver.kind === 'node:sqlite'. The defect is that this is unmeasured: any of the driver-shape assumptions the wrapper makes (RunResult number-vs-bigint, PRAGMA read-back shape, all()/get() return prototypes, WAL retry semantics) could regress in a Node minor and ship silently, on the exact path a user with no prebuilt binary or toolchain lands on.
remediation: Parameterize the driver-level suites over both drivers instead of testing one and documenting parity for two. A `vi.hoisted` Module._load stub (or a DRIVER env switch consumed by a `loadBetterSqlite` reset hook) is enough; skip only when node:sqlite is genuinely absent (Node < 22.5), and make that skip loud.
testUpgrade: Turn test/multi-process.test.ts's PRAGMAS table and test/at-rest-mode.test.ts's PRE_EXISTING table into `describe.each(['better-sqlite3','node:sqlite'])` suites, and add one seam round-trip (post -> fetchRecent -> subscribe -> disconnect) per driver. That guards the CLASS 'every driver the package can select at runtime is graded by the same assertions', so a third driver or a Node behaviour change cannot be certified by the incumbent's results.

summary: The comment 'Keep String() rather than a Number() round-trip, so that a 64-bit rowid cannot lose precision on the way to the dedup key' is false. better-sqlite3 returns lastInsertRowid — and every SELECTed INTEGER column — as a JS number unless safe-integers are enabled, so precision is already gone before String() sees it. The comment is written in exactly the 'keep X so that Y' form CLAUDE.md reserves for real hazards, so it would convince a maintainer that 64-bit rowids are handled.
failure: Reproduced directly against better-sqlite3 v12: inserting an explicit id 9007199254740993 and then a fresh row gives `lastInsertRowid = 9007199254740994 (typeof number)`, and `SELECT id` reads the first row back as 9007199254740992 while `CAST(id AS TEXT)` shows 9007199254740993. Above 2^53 that means post() and fetchRecent() disagree on backendMsgId for the same row, and the minted cursor `<store>.9007199254740992` re-selects that row forever (`id > 9007199254740992`) — a non-monotonic cursor and an infinite catch-up replay. Unreachable in practice via AUTOINCREMENT alone, but the comment claims the opposite of the truth.
remediation: Either make the claim true (enable safe integers on the driver — better-sqlite3 `defaultSafeIntegers(true)` / node:sqlite `setReadBigInts(true)` — and carry rowids as bigint through post/rowToMessage) or delete the comment and, per CLAUDE.md, record the reasoning in the commit message. A comment that overstates a guarantee is worse than none.
testUpgrade: Add a rowid-range table guarding the CLASS 'a rowid the store can hold round-trips identically through post(), fetchRecent() and the cursor': seed sqlite_sequence / explicit ids at [1, 2^31, 2^53-1, 2^53+1, 2^62] and for each assert post()'s returned backendMsgId equals the fetchRecent() backendMsgId for that row, and that fetching since that row's cursor returns zero rows. It will fail at 2^53+1 today, which is the honest signal about which range is actually supported.

summary: The 'SqlitePlugin (seam smoke)' block restates, more weakly, cases the shared conformance suite already runs against this exact plugin via test/conformance.test.ts. Five of its six cases cannot fail independently of a conformance case, so they cost runtime and reviewer attention while discriminating nothing — and they invite the next backend to copy the pattern, which is precisely what packages/conformance exists to prevent.
failure: Pairwise: 'post -> fetchRecent returns the message with a monotonic cursor' vs conformance 'post -> fetchRecent returns messages in order, with unique ids and distinct cursors'; 'fetchRecent({since}) is exclusive — only newer' vs 'catch-up since a cursor returns only newer messages (exclusive)'; 'topics are isolated' vs 'topics are isolated' (identical name and body shape); 'resolveIdentity uses the string convention' vs 'resolveIdentity answers for the handle it was asked about'; 'subscribe (poll loop) delivers new posts in order and skips history' vs 'subscribe delivers exactly the post-subscribe tail, once, in cursor order'. Any seam regression turns both red together; no mutation can turn only the local ones red. Only the sqlite-specific assertions inside them (cursor matches /^[0-9a-f]{16}\.N$/, backendMsgId === '1') are load-bearing.
remediation: Delete the five duplicated cases and keep only the sqlite-specific residue — fold the cursor-shape and rowid-value assertions into the existing 'SqlitePlugin backendMsgId' block. The seam contract is owned by packages/conformance; a backend package should only assert what is true of THIS backend and false of others.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS 'no backend package restates a conformance case' with a source-hygiene test (there is precedent: bridge-core/src/source-hygiene.test.ts): assert that every `it(...)` title in packages/*/src|test that is not the conformance runner has no near-duplicate in packages/conformance/src/index.ts, and that any backend test naming a seam method also asserts a backend-specific value (a cursor shape, an id format, a driver pragma). While there, collapse cursor-replay.test.ts's 4x4 store-reset matrix — the `before` dimension only varies the stale cursor's rowid, so [0,1,50] x [0,50] discriminates the same thing in 6 cases instead of 16.

summary: `concurrentPost` is the only multi-process check, and the conformance case that consumes it grades the result exclusively through fetchRecent/drainAll. Nothing in-tree asserts that the poll loop — the mechanism DESIGN §9 stakes 'the cursor guarantees nothing is missed' on — delivers every message committed by other OS processes. A poll loop that missed rows under concurrent commits would pass the whole suite.
failure: No wrong output today: I drove a live `subscribe` against 6 forked concurrent-writer.mjs processes x 80 messages each and all 480 arrived exactly once (`new Set(got).size === 480`), so the property holds. The gap is that it holds untested — the shipped suite's only subscribe-under-load case (background-jobs 'a full poll batch reschedules immediately') writes from the SAME process through the plugin's own prepared statement, so cross-process commit-vs-rowid ordering is never exercised on the live path.
remediation: Extend the conformance 'multi-process writes do not corrupt or error' case to attach a subscriber before calling ctx.concurrentPost and assert the live handler observed exactly the same backendMsgId set, in ascending cursor order, as drainAll — one assertion, no new fixture, and it applies to every backend that supplies a concurrentPost.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the CLASS 'both delivery paths agree under concurrent writers' in packages/conformance/src/index.ts over (writers, perWriter) = [(2,10),(4,25),(6,80)] with a subscriber armed BEFORE the writers start: assert live-delivered ids == catch-up ids for the post-subscribe suffix, with no duplicates and no gaps. That is a widened generator, so it also covers backends whose subscribe races their own writes.

summary: `retention_days` is validated for sign/finiteness/epoch range but not for whether `days * 86_400_000` is a whole number of milliseconds. Any value that is not a whole-millisecond window makes `Date.now() - retentionDays * 86_400_000` a float, which reaches Redis as a fractional `XADD ... MINID ~ <float>` and is rejected — so `connect()` succeeds and every single `post` fails, forever, with an error that names the topic and the Redis key but never `retention_days`.
failure: backend_config `{ url, retention_days: 30/7 }` (or `0.123456789`, `1/7`, `1e-6`) → `connect()` resolves; every `post(topic, handle, content)` rejects with `parley-redis: ERR Invalid stream ID specified as stream command argument (topic frac, key 'probe1:frac')`. Reproduced against redis:7-alpine on 6390. The whole durable write path — including presence heartbeats — is dead, and the diagnostic points the operator at a key collision.
remediation: Compute the threshold and reject at `connect()` unless it is an integer, e.g. `const ms = Math.round(value * 86_400_000)` and require `Number.isInteger(value * 86_400_000)` (or simply floor the threshold before it reaches `XADD`: `threshold: Math.floor(Date.now() - retentionDays * 86_400_000)`). Flooring is the smaller fix and cannot change any currently-working window; the validator message should still name `retention_days`.
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a backend_config value connect() ACCEPTS still breaks a seam call'. The existing `an accepted config still delivers` table only hand-picks values that happen to be integral (`0.5`, `7`, `30`). Replace it with a generator: for every knob, a property test over ~200 pseudo-random accepted values (for `retention_days`: `x/y` for small integers plus random floats in (0, maxDays]) that asserts `post → fetchRecent` round-trips. Add the same shape for `block_ms`/`connect_timeout_ms`. A single fixed row can never cover this class because the failure depends on the value's binary representation, not its magnitude.

summary: The seam's explicit plugin guarantee — `subscribe`'s handler fires in ascending cursor order, and `fetchRecent` returns messages already sorted ascending (seam.ts:11, :70) — is not pinned by any test on either of this plugin's batch-producing paths. Every case in the conformance suite and in failure-modes awaits each `post` sequentially, so every XREAD batch contains exactly one entry and the ordering assertions are tautologies.
failure: Mutating `for (const entry of stream.messages)` to `stream.messages.slice().reverse()` leaves all 211 tests green. Independently mutating `blockingRead`'s `return res[0]?.messages ?? []` to `.slice().reverse()` AND hard-coding `COUNT: 1` also leaves all 211 green. With the subscribe mutation live, subscribing then posting a real burst (`Promise.all` over 5 posts into a parked `XREAD BLOCK`) delivers `["m0","m4","m3","m2","m1","m4","m3","m2","m4","m3","m4"]` — descending within the batch, and duplicated because `lastId` ends up at the batch's lowest id. Bursts are the normal case under load, so core would emit `<channel>` events out of order and re-emit them.
remediation: No production change needed (the shipped code is correct); the guarantee needs to be pinned. Add burst cases that force multi-entry batches on both paths.
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a delivery path that can return N>1 messages is only ever graded on N==1'. Add to the SHARED conformance suite (so every backend inherits it), parameterized over burst size [2, 5, 25]: (a) subscribe, wait for the reader to park, then `await Promise.all(posts)` and assert the handler saw exactly the posted contents, once each, in posted order; (b) a blocking `fetchRecent({ since: tail, blockMs, limit: k })` woken by a concurrent burst of `k+2` posts — assert `messages.length <= k`, ascending order, `nextCursor === messages.at(-1).cursor`, and that resuming from `nextCursor` returns exactly the remainder. Both must also assert no duplicate `backendMsgId`, which is what catches the `lastId` regression this mutation exposed.

summary: `entryTimestamp` — the whole `ts`-field-or-stream-id-millisecond derivation — is untested for VALUE. The only assertions on `Message.timestamp` anywhere (conformance `expectWellFormedMessage`, and the foreign-writer table here) are `!Number.isNaN(Date.parse(...))`, which any constant satisfies. Three rows of the foreign-entry table (`an empty ts`, `a ts that is not a date`, `a numeric epoch ts`) differ only in that unasserted property, so they cannot independently fail and cost a live round trip each.
failure: Replacing the body of `entryTimestamp` with `return new Date(0).toISOString()` — deleting both the `ts` passthrough and the stream-id fallback — leaves all 211 tests green. Every message would report `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z` to the user and the suite would certify it.
remediation: Assert the derived value, not just its parseability: a plugin-written entry's timestamp must equal the `ts` field it wrote; a foreign entry with an unusable `ts` must fall back to the stream id's millisecond component (`new Date(Number(id.split('-')[0])).toISOString()`).
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a Message field asserted only for type/parseability, never for value'. In the shared conformance suite, widen `expectWellFormedMessage` to take an expected timestamp window and assert `Date.parse(m.timestamp)` falls between the wall-clock times bracketing the `post` call (plus backend slack) — that alone kills the epoch-0 mutation on every backend. In this package, collapse the three `ts` rows into one parameterized row carrying an `expectedTimestamp` (exact string, or a derivation function) so each row can fail for its own reason.

summary: `normalizeString('url', ...)` accepts any non-empty string, so an unparseable or wrong-scheme URL survives validation. `open()` then tears the previous connection down and only afterwards calls `createRedisClient`, which throws a bare `TypeError` naming neither the plugin nor the key — breaking the package's own stated contract that `connect()` 'rejects with an error naming the key rather than coercing', and leaving a previously-working plugin disconnected.
failure: `connect({ url: 'not a url' })` → `TypeError: Invalid URL`. `connect({ url: 'http://:hunter2@127.0.0.1:6390' })` → `TypeError: Invalid protocol`. Neither message contains `parley-redis`, `url`, or the offending value; an operator with a typo'd scheme (`redis//host`) has nothing to grep for. On a live plugin, the same call has already run `tearDown()`, so the bridge is left with no client and no subscriptions.
remediation: Parse the URL inside `normalizeString`/a dedicated `normalizeUrl`: require `new URL(value)` to succeed and its protocol to be `redis:`/`rediss:`, throwing the same `parley-redis: url must be …` shape as the other knobs. Do all validation (including this) before `await this.tearDown()`, so a rejected config never destroys a working connection.
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a config value that passes the declared validator and then fails somewhere unlabelled'. Extend the existing `rejectedByKnob` matrix for `url` beyond `NEVER_A_STRING` with a row set of non-empty-but-unusable strings (`'not a url'`, `'redis//127.0.0.1'`, `'http://h:1'`, `'redis+unix:///tmp/s'`, `' redis://h:1 '`), asserting the rejection matches `/^parley-redis: url/`. Add a companion invariant test asserting that a rejected `connect()` on an already-connected plugin leaves `post`/`fetchRecent` still working — that guards the teardown-ordering half of the class for every knob at once.

summary: `assertMintedCursor`'s JSDoc ends 'Throw labelled so core can drop it and refetch the window.' Core does no such thing. `catchUpTopic` rethrows anything that is not a `NoSuchTopicError`, and `fetchWithResumeHint` wraps the first resumed page in an operator-facing message telling them to delete the read-state file or change `instance_id`. The `parley_fetch_recent` tool likewise only catches `NoSuchTopicError`.
failure: Read-state holding a cursor minted by another backend (e.g. a Matrix `s123_456` after repointing `instance_id` at Redis) → `fetchRecent` throws → catch-up for that topic ABORTS with `catch-up failed on topic … Delete <state path> …`; nothing is 'dropped' and no window is refetched. A maintainer reading the plugin comment would believe the throw is self-healing and reason wrongly about the failure mode.
remediation: Delete the claim about core's behaviour from the comment (per CLAUDE.md, rationale about other layers belongs in the commit message), or restate it accurately: the throw is labelled so the operator can identify the plugin and topic. Note the deliberate asymmetry — a FUTURE-dated cursor self-heals silently, a foreign-format cursor is fatal — belongs in the README's cursor section if anywhere.
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a plugin comment/README asserts a behaviour that lives in another package'. Add a cross-layer test in this package that drives the real `catchUpTopic` (already exported from core) with a `RedisPlugin` whose read-state holds a foreign cursor, and pins the ACTUAL outcome (rejection, message shape). Any comment claiming core recovers then has an executable counterpart; the same shape can be reused for the stale-cursor self-heal, which core genuinely does tolerate.

summary: The README's `Run Redis` section ships a hardened recipe (loopback bind + `--requirepass`) and then offers, on the next line, '(or the maintainer dev harness: `examples/dev-compose/`.)' That compose publishes `6379:6379` on every interface with no password. `readme.test.ts`'s third CLASS block exists precisely to stop 'a shipped copy-pasteable artifact contradicting the package's own security guidance', but it scans only README URLs and `examples/multi-session/redis/*.yaml` — never the compose the README links.
failure: A reader following the README's own alternative runs `docker compose -f examples/dev-compose/docker-compose.yml up redis`, which (via Docker's own iptables rules, as this README warns) exposes an unauthenticated Redis holding every topic's full agent context and accepting forged-`sender` `XADD`s to anyone routable to the host — and the package's security test reports green.
remediation: Either bind the compose's redis port to `127.0.0.1:6379:6379` (the compose is framed as maintainer-only, so loopback costs nothing), or have the README state the exposure inline where it offers the harness rather than only in the section above.
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a security guard that lints only the artifacts it was written against, while the doc links others'. Widen `readme.test.ts` to derive its artifact set FROM THE README: extract every relative path/link the README mentions, resolve it, and apply the loopback+auth rules to any `docker run`/compose `ports:` entry found there. That way a future README that links a new example or compose automatically pulls it into the guard instead of silently escaping it.

summary: startSubscription publishes into this.subs AFTER an await with no `stopped` re-check, so a disconnect() landing while the LISTEN round-trip is in flight leaves a zombie TopicSubscription. The next connect() then sees it on subscribe()'s fast path and silently never LISTENs: push is permanently dead for that topic, with no error. Every other post-await publish in this class (adoptListener, the pool in connect) has the guard; this one, and subscribe()'s `finally { this.subscribing.delete(channel) }`, do not.
failure: connect(); subscribe('t', h) not awaited; disconnect() runs its synchronous teardown (subs/listens cleared) and parks in `await listener.end()`; the in-flight LISTEN resolves and line 553 runs this.subs.set(channel, sub). Measured with a gated pg mock: `subs after disconnect: 1  listens: 0`. Then connect(); subscribe('t', h2) resolves SUCCESSFULLY via the `live !== undefined` fast path at line 509 - measured `listens = 0, listener created? false, sub.handlers = [2]`. No LISTEN is ever issued and the listener connection is never even created, so no message posted to 't' is delivered to either handler for the life of the new session. Sibling shape: subscribe()'s `finally` deletes this.subscribing[channel] belonging to the NEW lifecycle, letting a third concurrent subscribe build a duplicate registration and inflate the LISTEN refcount.
remediation: Give the plugin a monotonic lifecycle epoch, captured at the top of connect() and compared before every post-await mutation of subs/subscribing/listens - not just `this.stopped`, which connect() resets to false. In startSubscription, after `await this.acquireListen(...)`, if the epoch moved, releaseListen and throw 'parley-postgres: disconnected while subscribe() was in flight' rather than registering. Guard subscribe()'s `finally` delete on the same epoch so it cannot evict a successor's entry.
testUpgrade: connection-hygiene.test.ts already drives the RaceCell matrix {opener: connect|subscribe|blocking-fetch|reconnect} x {in-flight|settled} but asserts only listener/listenerPromise/pool/backend-count. Widen its post-condition to the whole registry set (subs, subscribing, listens, waiters all empty after `await disconnect()`), and add a `then-reuse` axis to every cell: after disconnect, connect() again, subscribe(sameTopic), post, and assert the handler is actually fed within a deadline. That parameterization catches any state container the plugin grows later, not just `subs`.

summary: reconnectListener()'s `await delay(RECONNECT_DELAY_MS)` is not epoch-scoped and its only guard is `this.stopped`, which connect() resets to false. A reconnect loop sleeping when disconnect() lands therefore wakes INSIDE a new connect() lifecycle, connects, and calls adoptListener() - overwriting this.listener and this.listenerPromise and orphaning the new session's own listener connection, which is never end()ed.
failure: connect(); subscribe('t'); listener emits 'end' (server restart) -> reconnect loop enters its 500ms backoff; within that window disconnect(); connect(); subscribe('t'). Measured with a pg mock: 3 Client objects created, `listener changed: true`, and the listener the new session created and LISTENed on is left with `ended: false` while unreachable from the plugin. The subsequent disconnect() ends only the hijacker, so that socket and its server backend leak for the life of the process - exactly the property connection-hygiene.test.ts exists to protect, evaluated one lifecycle later than it looks.
remediation: Capture the lifecycle epoch when reconnectListener() starts and abort after every await if it changed (`if (epoch !== this.epoch) { await client.end().catch(()=>undefined); return; }`), with disconnect() flipping the epoch. Better still, make the backoff interruptible: bridge-net-util already has sleepUnlessStopped(ms, isStopped) - export it and use it here so disconnect() does not leave a live loop behind at all.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a 'a chore in flight when disconnect lands never touches the next lifecycle' matrix over every background loop the plugin runs {reconnect backoff, prune tick, drain loop, blocking-fetch wait} x {disconnect during the await, disconnect+connect during the await}, asserting in each cell that (a) no Client created before the disconnect is reachable from the plugin afterwards and (b) every Client ever constructed is either the current listener or ended. lifecycle.test.ts's existing reconnect-race case stops at disconnect and never re-connects, which is why it misses this.

summary: The cursor returned for an empty since-less page - `args.since ?? asCursor('0')` - is completely unpinned by the suite. Mutating that constant to a value above the live sequence keeps all 333 tests green, including the full @sharptrick/parley-conformance suite run twice against a real PostgreSQL server. A regression here silently loses every message below the bogus cursor, which is the exact failure the cursor contract exists to prevent.
failure: Mutation: `nextCursor = last !== undefined ? last.cursor : (args.since ?? asCursor('999999'))`. Full run against postgres:16-alpine: `Test Files 15 passed, Tests 333 passed`. Live consequence: a bridge doing catch-up-on-start against a topic with no rows yet persists nextCursor='999999'; every subsequent post (seq 1..999999) is invisible to fetchRecent forever, with no error. Conformance's 'fetchRecent on a never-posted topic returns an empty page with a replayable cursor' only replays the cursor against the still-empty topic, so a cursor that is replayable AND ahead of everything passes it.
remediation: The constant is currently correct; the gap is the guard. Add the missing property to the package suite (and propose it for the frozen conformance suite, which shares the hole with every backend): a cursor obtained from an EMPTY topic must still deliver messages posted afterwards.
testUpgrade: Ratchet the class, not the constant: parameterize over {empty topic, topic drained to its tail} x {0, 1, 5, DRAIN_BATCH+1 messages posted afterwards} - take nextCursor from a fetch that returned an empty page, post N messages, and assert fetchRecent({since: thatCursor}) returns exactly those N in order with nextCursor equal to the last one's. The empty-topic arm is the one no existing case reaches; it is what makes any 'cursor invented for an empty page' mutation visible.

summary: Every write to the `<table>_senders` registry can be deleted with the whole suite staying green - it is unguarded, and behaviourally write-only: resolveIdentity's fallback returns {handle, backendRef: handle}, identical to the only row the plugin can ever have written. The upsert also sits inside post()'s advisory-lock-held transaction, lengthening the critical section every same-topic post from every bridge process queues behind, for a row nothing reads.
failure: Deleted both `INSERT INTO <table>_senders ... ON CONFLICT (handle) DO NOTHING` statements (post() line 351 and resolveIdentity() line 570). Full run against postgres:16-alpine: `Test Files 15 passed, Tests 333 passed`. Nothing in the package - not conformance's 'resolveIdentity answers for the handle it was asked about', not table-name.test.ts's `expect(await plugin.resolveIdentity(asHandle('alice'))).toEqual({handle:'alice',backendRef:'alice'})` - can distinguish a populated registry from an empty one, because the fallback produces the same answer. The DDL that creates the table is equally unasserted.
remediation: Either assert the registry's one observable behaviour (pre-populate a row with backend_ref != handle and require resolveIdentity to return it - the operator-facing extension point README line 18 implies), or, if that is not a supported feature, move the upsert out of post()'s locked transaction so the serialized write path carries only the INSERT it exists for.
testUpgrade: Add a table-driven registry case parameterized over {handle never seen, handle seen only via post(), handle pre-registered with a distinct backend_ref, handle registered concurrently by two plugin instances}, asserting both the returned backendRef and the row count in `<table>_senders`. The distinct-backend_ref row is what makes every registry write mutation-visible; without it, any table this plugin creates but never reads can be deleted invisibly.

summary: The suite restates its harness in every file instead of sharing it, and carries one real-server case twice. `async function isUp(url)` appears in 8 files, `async function dropTable(table)` in 6, and 7 files hand-roll their own vi.mock('pg') Pool/Client factory (only fake-pg.ts's SELECT server is shared) - so the mocks have already drifted: background-tasks.test.ts's pool ignores servePool and returns [] for every windowed SELECT, making its post-failure recovery assertion weaker than it reads.
failure: config-validation.test.ts:170 'a valid retention window prunes, and the cursor still advances past what it removed' and retention.test.ts:39 row 'prunes older rows when set to a real window' are the same test: seed 3 posts, connect with retention_days: 1/86_400_000, sleep, expect 0 messages, post 'after-prune', expect it last and Number(fresh) > 3. Neither can fail without the other failing; each costs a real-server round trip plus its sleep, and a reviewer cannot tell which file owns the property.
remediation: Extract the real-server harness (isUp, withAdmin, dropTable, settledBackendCount, the `if (await isUp(PG_URL))` gate) into test/pg-harness.ts, and the pg module mock into a single test/mock-pg.ts factory parameterized by the knobs files actually vary (listen mode/delay, connect gate, pool failure, row table). Delete the duplicated retention case from config-validation.test.ts; retention.test.ts owns it.
testUpgrade: The remedy is merging, not adding. Guard the class with a source-hygiene assertion in the style of bridge-core/src/source-hygiene.test.ts: no test file in this package other than test/mock-pg.ts may call vi.mock('pg'), and the real-server gate must come from test/pg-harness.ts - so the next file added cannot fork a fake that quietly serves weaker semantics than servePool.

summary: README line 23 states the channel name is `'parley_' || md5(topic)`. The trigger deliberately does not do that - schema.ts:151 is `md5(convert_to(NEW.topic, 'UTF8'))`, and schema.ts:118-121 plus the whole of notify-channel.test.ts exist because the bare form silently kills the live path on a non-UTF8 server_encoding. The public claim documents exactly the spelling the code was fixed away from.
failure: An operator reading the README and writing their own LISTEN client, or an off-Parley NOTIFY producer, against a LATIN1 database computes md5('cafe' with an accented e) over LATIN1 bytes, gets a different digest from channelFor()'s UTF-8 digest, and the doorbell rings a channel nobody LISTENs: push delivers nothing, blocking fetches stall their whole budget, catch-up keeps working, nothing errors. Same file, line 51 has a second inaccuracy: the prune is claimed to run 'in batches of 5000 rows per statement against an index on ts', but the statement is `WHERE seq IN (SELECT seq ... WHERE ts < $1 ORDER BY seq LIMIT 5000)` - the ORDER BY seq is what the planner satisfies, so the named index is not the access path.
remediation: Change line 23 to `'parley_' || md5(convert_to(topic, 'UTF8'))` and state in one clause that the explicit cast is what keeps the Node and server digests equal on a non-UTF8 database. Correct or drop the 'against an index on ts' claim on line 51.
testUpgrade: Guard the class rather than the sentence: add a docs case that extracts every fenced and inline SQL fragment from packages/bridge-postgres/README.md and asserts each appears verbatim in buildSchema()'s output or in a query string in src/, so future README SQL that drifts from what ships fails the build. notify-channel.test.ts already pins the DDL side (`expect(ddl).toMatch(/md5\(\s*convert_to\(/)`) - it just never looks at the README.

summary: CLAUDE.md admits a comment only as a 'keep X, so that Y' warning off a risky action; rationale belongs in the commit message. The drain fan-out states the same thing twice five lines apart, and several comments restate the line below them.
failure: index.ts:744-745 `// Fan out to every handler on this channel, each best-effort in its own try/catch so one throwing handler can't starve the others (DESIGN 6).` is repeated in substance at :750 `/* handler is best-effort; never break the loop (DESIGN 6) */` inside the very catch it describes. Likewise :301 `// Transient contention/connection failure - retry on the next interval.` and :239 `/* idle-client errors ... don't crash */` narrate what the empty catch already says, and the class JSDoc at :168-176 ('Slots between SQLite ... and Redis ...') is positioning prose duplicated from the README, not a risk warning. By contrast :368-369 (the ORDER BY output-alias trap) is exactly the kind that earns its place.
remediation: Delete the duplicate at :750 and the restating comments at :239 and :301. Keep the positioning paragraph only in the README and reduce the class JSDoc to its risk clause (the doorbell-is-not-the-cursor invariant). Keep :368-369 unchanged.
testUpgrade: The mechanical half is guardable: extend the repo's source-hygiene test (packages/bridge-core/src/source-hygiene.test.ts) with a rule applied across all packages that no two comments within one function body may share a normalized token set - that catches the duplicated-comment class wherever it recurs rather than this instance.

summary: Every empty-result exit of `blockingFetch` returns `nextCursor: sinceCursor`, throwing away the anti-wedge advance that `fetchSince`/`drainForward` just computed. With `block_ms` set, the cursor can therefore never cross a foreign-topic block, and the same query returns a different cursor depending only on `blockMs`.
failure: shared_room mode, limit=5. (a) post a0 to topic A, then 20 messages to topic B: `fetchRecent({topic:A, since:a0, limit:5})` → nextCursor `$e19` (advanced), but `fetchRecent({topic:A, since:a0, limit:5, blockMs:120})` → nextCursor `$e0` (unchanged). (b) post a0, then 300 topic-B messages, then a1: draining with `blockMs:120` four times (core's `fetchRecentBlocking` feeds `nextCursor` back as `since`) returns `[]` every time — a1 is beyond MAX_FORWARD_PAGES*limit=250 and the cursor never moves, so it is unreachable forever; without blockMs the same drain returns ['a1']. Reproduced against the in-repo fake.
remediation: Thread the best-known cursor through `blockingFetch`: seed it with `first.nextCursor` from `fetchRecent`, replace it with `recheck.nextCursor`/`after.nextCursor` on every empty re-query, and return that (not the caller's `since`) on timeout, stale-generation and pre-park exits. README's "`nextCursor` advances past a page-sized block of foreign-topic traffic so it can never wedge" then becomes true on both paths.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the existing FOREIGN_BLOCKS table in test/catchup-sync.fake.test.ts over `blockMs ∈ {0, 150}` and assert the returned `nextCursor` is IDENTICAL for both — the class is "a blocking call must report the same position a non-blocking one would". Add a widened row with a foreign block deeper than MAX_FORWARD_PAGES*limit driven through `fetchRecentBlocking` (core's real driver) asserting the on-topic tail is eventually drained, so the bound cannot be silently re-introduced by any future early-return.

summary: `joinRoom` passes `allowStatuses: [403]` and ignores the response, so "you are not invited to this room" is treated as a successful join. With the default `room_preset: private_chat` (join_rule invite) and the default empty `invite`, a second Matrix account is silently locked out and the failure only surfaces later as an opaque 403 from `/send` and `/messages`.
failure: Against a real Synapse (throwaway, port 8009): alice posts to topic `multi-x` → room created invite-only. bob (a distinct account, exactly what the README prescribes) connects and posts the same topic → `lookupAlias` 200, `joinRoom` 403 swallowed, then `post` throws `Matrix PUT .../send/... → 403 {"errcode":"M_FORBIDDEN","error":"User @bob:parley.local not in room ..."}`. bob's `fetchRecent` throws the same 403 ("and room previews are disabled") — which `catchUpAll` propagates, so bob's bridge cannot even start. bob's `subscribe` is worse: /sync succeeds and simply never yields the room, so the live path is silently dead with no error at all.
remediation: Make the join fail fast and legibly: check the join response and, on 403, throw naming the alias, the MXID and the fix ("add this account to `invite`, or have the room's creator invite it"). Alternatively auto-invite peers — but the silent-success branch must go either way, and `subscribe` must not register a live route for a room it is not joined to.
testUpgrade: CLASS: no seam call may proceed on a swallowed authorization failure. Table-drive over {post, fetchRecent, subscribe} x {join→403, join→404} in the fake (give FakeSynapse a `joinStatus` knob) asserting each rejects with an error naming the room alias and the account, and that `subscribe` does not add to `liveTopics`. Add a live two-account case (register a second Synapse user in examples/dev-compose/dev-infra.sh, as the XMPP path already does) covering create-by-A → post/read/subscribe-by-B.

summary: The README's "Multiple concurrent sessions" section insists each session use a DIFFERENT Matrix account and links `examples/multi-session/matrix` as the runnable example — but none of the three shipped configs sets `invite`, and the default preset makes every provisioned room invite-only. Following the documented layout verbatim produces a deployment where only the first session works.
failure: `examples/multi-session/matrix/code-agent-a.yaml` (user `parley-agent-a`) and `code-agent-b.yaml` (user `parley-agent-b`) both list topic `ctx-infra`; neither sets `invite`. Whichever starts first creates `#parley_ctx-infra:parley.local` with join_rule invite; the other's startup catch-up rejects with 403 M_FORBIDDEN and its live path silently delivers nothing (reproduced against real Synapse with two accounts).
remediation: Add `invite: ["@parley-agent-b:parley.local", "@parley-owner:parley.local"]` (and the symmetric lists) to the example configs, and state in the README's multi-session section that with the default preset every account that is not the room creator must appear in some creator's `invite` list — the invite requirement is currently only mentioned in the unrelated "topic rooms are invite-only" section.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a shipped example config must be executable, not illustrative. Extend the existing examples/**/*.test.ts coverage with a Matrix case that loads all three multi-session configs, asserts the `user` values are pairwise distinct AND that every other config's derived MXID appears in at least one config's `invite` (a pure config-consistency check that needs no homeserver), plus a gated live case that starts two plugins from those two configs and requires both to post and read the shared topic.

summary: `readRetryAfter` — the entire 429/`M_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` handling — is vacuously covered. Replacing its body with `return 500` leaves the whole matrix suite green, even though FakeSynapse ships `createRoomLimited`/`createRoomRetryAfterMs` knobs built precisely to exercise it.
failure: Mutation: `async function readRetryAfter(res) { void res; return 500; }` → `npx vitest run packages/bridge-matrix` → 12 files / 174 tests all pass. A regression that ignored Synapse's `retry_after_ms` entirely — the one thing standing between the bridge and a room-creation ban under the ~2-room burst limit the README documents — would ship unnoticed.
remediation: Add a 429 case that drives `post` on an unprovisioned topic with `createRoomLimited = 1` and asserts (i) the create is retried and eventually succeeds, and (ii) the wait actually taken matches the server's stated `retry_after_ms` (inject a clock/`delay` spy rather than sleeping).
testUpgrade: CLASS: every hint-extraction function must be killed by a mutation to a constant. Table-drive over the shapes the wire can carry — `Retry-After` header in seconds, `Retry-After` as an HTTP-date, `retry_after_ms` in the body, both present, neither present, zero/negative values — asserting the ms the retry loop actually waits for each row. The same table shape retires the identical gap in the sibling backends' `readRetryAfter`.
