summary: `readRetryAfter` caps a SERVER-STATED wait at 5s and returns a hardcoded 500 instead of `undefined` when there is no hint — both contrary to `fetchWithRetry`'s documented contract ("Honour a server-stated wait IN FULL … Only a wait we invented is clamped"). bridge-discord and bridge-zulip return `undefined` and do not cap; matrix (with telegram) is the outlier.
failure: Synapse answers `POST /createRoom` with 429 `retry_after_ms: 45000`. `readRetryAfter` returns 5000, so `fetchWithRetry` sees a "stated" 5s wait and retries roughly every 5s until its 30s deadline — about 6 attempts against a limiter that asked for 45s — then throws the generic "still rate limited after N attempts". Honouring 45000 would trip `overDeadline` on the first 429 and produce the actionable message the shared module was written to emit ("upstream asked for 45000ms, past this call's 30000ms deadline. Raise deadlineMs to wait it out"). Secondary: because the function never returns `undefined`, `retryAfterFromHeader`'s RFC 9110 HTTP-date branch is unreachable and hint-less 429s bypass `clampBackoff`.
remediation: Return `undefined` when no usable hint exists and return the server's value uncapped when one does — matching discord/zulip and letting `fetchWithRetry`'s deadline be the single governor, as its JSDoc says.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a per-backend `retryAfterOf` must not narrow the shared policy. One parameterized test in bridge-net-util's suite (or a shared helper) run over every backend's exported `readRetryAfter`: for a 429 carrying a 45s hint the returned value must be >= the hint, and for a 429 carrying no hint it must be `undefined`.

summary: `connect()` resets `stopped`, `generation` and `rooms` but not `liveTopics`, and `subscribe` adds its (room, topic) key without an `isStale` check. A subscribe loop that has stood down therefore leaves a permanent phantom "a live loop covers this pair" entry, and a later blocking `fetchRecent` trusts it and refuses to open its own dedicated /sync.
failure: Reproduced on the fake, two reachable shapes. (a) `connect(); subscribe(T); connect(fakeConfig())` (no disconnect — the reconnect the plugin's own generation counter exists to support) leaves `liveTopics = ['!room:fake\0T']`; a subsequent `fetchRecent({topic:T, since:tail, blockMs:3000})` with `sync_timeout_ms: 8000` returns the message that landed at t=150ms only at t=3006ms instead of ~176ms (measured; with `catchup.block_max_ms` 60s in production the delay is a full slice of `sync_timeout_ms`). (b) `const s = subscribe(T); await disconnect(); await s;` — disconnect clears the set, then the in-flight subscribe re-adds the key after it, so the phantom survives even the clean teardown path.
remediation: Clear `liveTopics` in `connect()` alongside `rooms`, and have `subscribe` skip the registration (and the loop) when `isStale(generation)` after its awaits — or key the registration on the generation so a stale entry can never match.
testUpgrade: CLASS: no registry entry may outlive the work it describes. Extend test/reconnect-lifecycle.fake.test.ts (already the "nothing survives disconnect + connect" file) with a table over lifecycle sequences — {subscribe→disconnect→connect, subscribe→connect, disconnect-racing-subscribe} x {liveTopics, waiters, controllers, rooms} — asserting every internal registry is empty after the sequence, plus a behavioural row asserting a blocking fetchRecent still wakes in << blockMs afterwards.

summary: The provisioning table asserts `preset` and `invite` on the createRoom body but never `visibility`, so the directory-privacy half of the security story is prose-only.
failure: Mutation: `visibility: 'private'` → `visibility: 'public'` in `resolveOrCreateRoom` → whole matrix suite green (174/174). Every topic room would then be listed in the homeserver's public (federated) room directory, publishing the deployment's topic names — a regression the suite cannot see.
remediation: Assert the full createRoom body shape in the existing table (`visibility: 'private'`, `preset` from config, `invite` from config, `room_alias_name` derived from the topic) rather than field-by-field on a couple of rows.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a security-relevant request body is asserted whole, not by spot-check. Snapshot/compare the entire `createRoomBodies[0]` object against an expected object in each row of the existing shared/per-topic x entry-point x aliasExists table, so any silently added, removed or flipped field fails.

summary: The live conformance fixture runs exclusively in `shared_room` mode with a single account — the mode the README says "MUST NOT" be used in production. The production configuration (one room per topic, several accounts) is never exercised against a real homeserver by anything, and `examples/dev-compose/dev-infra.sh` registers only one Matrix user (the XMPP path deliberately registers two).
failure: All 25 live conformance cases passed against my throwaway Synapse while the per-topic-room, multi-account path was broken end to end (see the join-403 finding) — the suite structurally cannot observe it. The only per-topic live assertion in the package is the join_rules probe in provisioning.fake.test.ts, which uses one account.
remediation: Register a second Matrix user in dev-infra.sh and add a small live per-topic-room suite (or a second conformance context whose `freshTopic` count fits the room-creation burst) covering create-by-A / read-write-by-B; keep the shared_room fixture for the rate-limit-bound bulk.
testUpgrade: CLASS: the conformance context must cover the configuration the README calls production. Parameterize the matrix conformance factory over `{shared_room: set, shared_room: unset}` and run the second variant with a reduced topic count (or an `it.each` guard on the creation budget), so the mode that ships is graded by the same frozen suite.

summary: `fetchRecent` computes its deadline before branching on `since` and passes it to `roomForRead`, so a since-LESS call honours `blockMs` by waiting for the room to be provisioned. The seam docstring says the opposite: "Blocking only engages relative to a `since`; with no `since` the default recent window returns at once."
failure: `parley_fetch_recent({topic: <allowlisted but never posted>, block_ms: 60000})` with no `since` — a call a model can make, on a topic pattern-matched from untrusted context — pins the MCP tool call for the full 60s inside the plugin instead of returning the empty recent window immediately (core's wrapper would nap and re-poll, giving the caller the same budget but the documented immediate first answer).
remediation: Pass `deadline` to `roomForRead` only when `args.since !== undefined`; a since-less read should use `existingRoom` and return the empty window at once. If the wait is genuinely wanted, change the seam docstring instead — but it is frozen, so the plugin should follow it.
testUpgrade: CLASS: `blockMs` must engage only where the seam says it does. Add a shared conformance case (it belongs in packages/conformance, so every native-blocking backend is graded): for a never-posted topic, `fetchRecent({topic, blockMs: 2000})` with no `since` must return within a small fraction of the budget, while the same call WITH a tail `since` may block.

summary: FakeSynapse's `createRoomLimited` / `createRoomRetryAfterMs` model the 429 room-creation limiter, but no test ever takes that branch: the single use sets `createRoomLimited = Infinity` in a case that asserts ZERO createRoom calls, so the 429 response body is never produced and `createRoomRetryAfterMs` is never read.
failure: `grep createRoomLimited test/*.test.ts` → one hit, in the "a read on an unprovisioned topic" case whose own assertion is `expect(fake.createRoomBodies).toHaveLength(0)`. A reader takes the knob as evidence the rate-limit path is covered; the mutation above shows it is not.
remediation: Either add the retry case the knob was built for (see the readRetryAfter finding) or delete both knobs — fixture surface with no case is coverage theatre.
testUpgrade: CLASS: no fault-injection knob without a case that observes it firing. Give FakeSynapse an assertion-time audit (as it already does for `stalledPositioning`/`limitedEmitted`) — e.g. a `usedFaults` set — and add one test that fails if a knob was armed but its branch never executed, so the pattern generalizes to `messagesFailures`, `syncFailures` and any future injector.

summary: The rationale for never minting `''` as a cursor is written out four times — the `STREAM_CURSOR_PREFIX` docblock (l.73-78), the `since === ''` branch comment in `fetchSince` (l.301-303), the `nextCursor` comment in `recentWindow` (l.600-602), and the README's cursor row. Three of them restate the same causal chain ("'' 404s on /context → decoded as expired → drops everything older than the recent window").
failure: Not a runtime failure: it is four copies that can disagree. A change to the expired-cursor fallback has to be reflected in four places or the code acquires three confident, wrong explanations — exactly what CLAUDE.md routes to the commit message.
remediation: Keep the risk warning once, on `STREAM_CURSOR_PREFIX`, and let the two call-site comments shrink to a reference or disappear; move the measured/decided history to the commit message. The README row stays, as it is the published contract.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a single rationale should not be restated across sites. Extend test/comment-hygiene.test.ts (already the "comments carry no tracker history" gate) with a duplicate-prose check: normalize comment text per source file and fail when the same >=12-word span appears in more than one comment block, so the class is caught wherever it recurs rather than at this one phrase.

summary: An identity.handle longer than the nick fold's 64-char truncation makes safeName throw, so every post() on the plugin rejects permanently with an error about topic collisions.
failure: post(topic, asHandle('a'.repeat(70)), 'hi') rejects with `Error: safeName built "aaaa…-ed6c69d9e8" … but this backend's fold rewrites it to "aaaa…": the disambiguating suffix does not survive the backend name rules`. sanitizeNick truncates to 64, so sanitized !== raw, so safeName appends `-<10 hex>` making a 75-char name, which sanitizeNick re-truncates to 64 and safeName rejects. Because nickFor throws synchronously inside `this.nickAdoption ??= this.switchNick(nickFor(identity))`, nickAdoption is never assigned and EVERY subsequent post throws the same way. Threshold is 65 chars for an all-legal handle and 54 for a handle containing any char outside [A-Za-z0-9.\-_]. bridge-core's config schema only requires `identity.handle` to be `z.string().min(1)`, so this is a legal config that bricks the backend. The README claims the opposite: "`topic` and `identity` are folded to a legal charset instead, injectively, so they cannot collide."
remediation: Make the fold's own truncation leave room for the suffix: `sanitizeNick = s => s.replace(/[^A-Za-z0-9.\-_]/g, '_').slice(0, 64 - 1 - MIN_HASH_LEN)` so `safeName`'s output is a fixed point of the fold for every input length. Either way, wrap nickFor so a fold failure surfaces as a named parley-xmpp error rather than core's collision message, and fix the README sentence if any input is still refused rather than folded.
testUpgrade: Class = "a backend name fold whose own length/charset limit makes safeName's disambiguating suffix unrepresentable". Add a parameterized case in sender-identity.test.ts driving nickFor/roomJid over a generated handle+topic table crossing lengths {1, 53, 54, 63, 64, 65, 200, 2000} with charsets {ascii-legal, contains-space, contains-slash, non-ascii, astral emoji}, asserting each yields a non-empty legal nick, that distinct inputs yield distinct nicks, and that no input throws. The existing xml-hostile-content 'post identity (adopted as the MUC nick)' row is the near-miss: it crosses the charset axis but every payload is short, so the length axis is unreached.

summary: onOccupancyLost re-joins immediately with no backoff, no cap and no rate-limited logging, so a room that ends occupancy on every join turns into an unbounded join-presence and stderr flood.
failure: With a subscribed room whose server answers each join presence with self-presence and then `<presence type='unavailable'><status code='307'/>`, the plugin emitted 410 join presences in 500 ms (~820/s) and one console.error per iteration, and does not stop. Trace: onOccupancyLost -> ensureJoinedRoom -> doJoin -> joinOnce sends the presence synchronously; doJoin's `delay(100 + 100*attempt)` only covers RETRYABLE_CONDITIONS on a *rejected* join, and this join succeeds every time. Real triggers: a moderation bot that kicks the bridge, a members-only room (322) toggling, a flapping MUC component, and status 332 "MUC service shutting down" — where the bridge hammers a service that is deliberately going away. The server's own rate limiter then drops the c2s stream, @xmpp/reconnect re-establishes, and the cycle resumes. reportStreamError has a STREAM_ERROR_LOG_MS floor; this path has none.
remediation: Give the occupancy-lost re-join the same bounded, backing-off treatment doJoin gives a retryable condition: per-room exponential backoff with a ceiling and a jitter, a cap on consecutive re-entries within a window after which the room is left un-joined with one loud error, and rate-limit the `occupancy in X ended` log the way reportStreamError is rate-limited. Status 332 in particular should back off hard rather than retry immediately.
testUpgrade: Class = "remote-driven recovery with no backoff or cap". Extend membership-revalidation.test.ts's loss table with a `repeat: true` axis so each loss route (307/301/321/322/332/destroy/silent-forget/bounced-post) can be replayed on every successful join, and assert an upper bound on join presences sent within a fixed window (e.g. <= 10 in 1 s) and on console.error calls. Today every row loses occupancy exactly once, which is precisely the shape that cannot observe a storm.

summary: Both safeName folds — topic->MUC room and handle->MUC nick — can be deleted outright and the entire package suite stays green; the injectivity core exists to provide is verified nowhere for this plugin.
failure: Mutation 1: `roomJid` -> `` `${sanitizeLocal(topic)}@${this.mucService}` `` (safeName removed). Result: 15 test files, all pass. Topics 'Ops' and 'ops', or 'dev ops' and 'dev/ops', then share one MUC room, so one topic's traffic is delivered under another topic's name — a topic-allowlist bypass and cross-topic history leak. Mutation 2: `nickFor` -> `sanitizeNick(String(identity))`. Result: 15 test files, all pass. Handles 'a b' and 'a_b' become one occupant nick, so two agents collapse into one sender in every archived message and in parley_list_users. bridge-core/src/topic-name.test.ts appears to cover this but does not: it re-declares its own private copies of each backend's regex and never imports the plugin, so neither mutation can reach it. The source comments assert both properties ("The fold is injective via safeName, so two handles can never land on one occupant identity").
remediation: Add package-local injectivity assertions that call the plugin's real code paths (roomJid via priv(), and the nick actually sent on the join presence), rather than relying on core's copied-regex test.
testUpgrade: Class = "a backend's legal-charset fold whose injectivity is asserted only against a copy of the regex". Add one parameterized case per fold over a colliding-pair table — ('Ops','ops'), ('a/b','a_b'), ('a b','a_b'), ('team.frontend','team_frontend'), plus a pair of the form (X, sanitize(X)+'-'+sha1(X)[0:10]) that probes safeName's isDisambiguated branch — asserting roomJid(p) !== roomJid(q) and that the join presence's nick differs for the corresponding handle pairs. Widen it to a generator that samples random strings, sanitizes them, and asserts no two distinct topics/handles ever produce one room/nick.

summary: connect() casts backend_config unchecked, so a misspelled key is silently ignored and a wrong-typed value surfaces as an opaque TypeError — deviating from the validateBackendConfig pattern bridge-sqlite and bridge-postgres already ship.
failure: `backend_config: { muc_servce: 'muc.example.com' }` (one transposed letter) -> connect() resolves silently and every room is addressed at the default `muc.parley.local`; on a real server the join bounces `remote-server-not-found`, which is in RETRYABLE_CONDITIONS, so the operator gets ~4 s of silent retries and then a JoinError that never names the typo. `backend_config: { mam_page: '5' }` (a YAML-quoted number) -> mamPageOf sees a non-number, Number.isFinite('5') is false, and the value is silently replaced by 200. `backend_config: { nick: 123 }` -> `TypeError: s is not iterable` out of xmlIllegalCodepoint's for-of, naming neither the plugin nor the key. DESIGN.md line 477 documents the xmpp block as `{ service, jid, password, muc_service }`, so an operator following DESIGN writes `jid:` — silently ignored, falling back to username 'parley' and the default password. bridge-core deliberately leaves backend_config open (config.ts:186) precisely because each plugin is supposed to validate it, and its own comment says unknown keys must be a load error "or a misspelled key would otherwise leave the operator with a bridge that quietly does nothing".
remediation: Add `validateBackendConfig(config): XmppBackendConfig` modelled on packages/bridge-sqlite/src/index.ts:407-462 — reject unknown keys naming the accepted set, and type/range-check service, domain, muc_service, username, password, nick (string, non-empty) and mam_page (positive integer) with `parley-xmpp: invalid backend_config.<key> — …` errors, before client() is constructed.
testUpgrade: Class = "plugin backend_config accepted by unchecked cast". Add a table-driven case crossing every declared key with {missing, correct, misspelled-key, wrong-type (number/bool/null/array/object), empty string, out-of-range} and assert each non-correct cell rejects with an error naming both 'parley-xmpp' and the key, and that no cell throws a bare TypeError. Since this class recurs across every backend, the same table shape belongs in the shared conformance context so a plugin that omits validation cannot certify.

summary: The `<history maxstanzas='0'/>` join hint — the plugin's only defence against a MUC replaying room history as live push — can be deleted with the whole suite (and even the live conformance run) staying green.
failure: Mutation: `xml('x', { xmlns: NS_MUC }, xml('history', { maxstanzas: '0' }))` -> `xml('x', { xmlns: NS_MUC })`. Result: 15 fake-based test files pass. The live conformance case that names this guarantee ('subscribe delivers exactly the post-subscribe tail, once, in cursor order') cannot catch it either, because its subscribe() reuses the join the earlier posts already cached, so no join presence is ever sent while a subscriber is attached. The paths where it actually bites are exactly the re-join paths — reconnect and every occupancy-loss route — where a MUC with default history settings would push N archived messages back through onGroupchat as live stanzas, re-firing every long-poll waiter and re-delivering to every subscriber (core dedups on backendMsgId, but DESIGN and the README state the plugin must not replay history as live). FakeXmpp.onJoin never replays, so the fixture cannot express the failure.
remediation: Teach FakeXmpp.onJoin to replay the room's archive as live groupchat stanzas unless the join presence carries `<history maxstanzas='0'/>`, i.e. model what a real MUC does, then the guard becomes load-bearing.
testUpgrade: Class = "a protocol hint whose absence is only observable on a re-entry path the fixture never exercises". Parameterize membership-revalidation.test.ts's existing loss table with an assertion that after each recovery the subscriber saw no message it had already seen (compare backendMsgId sets before and after the loss), with the fake replaying history on any join that does not request maxstanzas=0. That one axis covers reconnect, kick, ban, 321/322/332, destroy and silent-forget at once.

summary: A seam call after disconnect() leaves a pendingJoins entry and an armed 15 s timer behind, violating the package's own expectNoLeaks invariant.
failure: connect -> post -> disconnect -> post again: the second post rejects correctly, but priv(plugin).pendingJoins.size is 1 afterwards and expectNoLeaks fails. Trace: joinOnce registers `entry` and arms the JOIN_TIMEOUT_MS timer, then `this.require()` throws synchronously because this.xmpp is undefined; the executor's throw rejects the promise without ever running `settle`, so neither clearTimeout nor the map delete happen. The slot self-clears only when the 15 s timer fires — which also keeps the Node event loop alive for 15 s past shutdown, and leaves a live correlator that any stray self-presence for that room would resolve. The conformance case 'disconnect is idempotent and stops the plugin serving' drives exactly this sequence and asserts nothing about leaks.
remediation: Fail fast before registering: check `this.stopped`/`this.xmpp === undefined` at the top of joinOnce (and of post/fetchRecent/subscribe) and reject without arming anything; or move the `this.require()` call above the pendingJoins.set + setTimeout, or wrap the send in a try/catch that calls entry.reject.
testUpgrade: Class = "an operation registering a keyed correlator and a timer before the step that can fail synchronously". Add a parameterized case crossing every seam entry point {post, fetchRecent, fetchRecent+blockMs, subscribe, resolveIdentity} with every pre-broken state {never connected, after disconnect, disconnect racing an in-flight call}, asserting each rejects AND that expectNoLeaks holds AND vi.getTimerCount() is 0. pending-registry.test.ts already owns the registry-invariant vocabulary but only exercises the connected path.

summary: disconnect()'s cancellation of in-flight long-polls is asserted by no test: removing the fire('cancel') loop leaves the suite fully green, despite a source comment claiming it prevents leaked listeners and timers.
failure: Mutation: delete `for (const set of [...this.waiters.values()]) for (const fire of [...set]) fire('cancel');` from disconnect(), keeping only `this.waiters.clear()`. Result: 15 test files pass. With the mutation, a `fetchRecent({blockMs: 60000})` parked at the time of shutdown holds its 60 s timer to expiry instead of returning at once, so the process cannot exit and cli.ts's shutdown path is left waiting on a bridge that has already stopped. Every existing long-poll case either lets the budget expire or is woken by a message; none disconnects mid-park.
remediation: None needed in src — this is a coverage gap. Ratchet it so the comment's claim is enforced.
testUpgrade: Class = "a teardown path that must settle in-flight waiters, with no test that has an in-flight waiter at teardown". Add a parameterized case in long-poll-wake.test.ts that starts a blocking fetch with a large blockMs, calls disconnect() at t in {0ms, 10ms, mid-query-round-trip via onMamInFlight}, and asserts the fetch resolves within a small bound with an empty page and the caller's cursor, that expectNoLeaks holds, and that vi.getTimerCount() is 0. Same axis applies to a subscribe and a pending post.

summary: DESIGN.md documents the xmpp backend_config as `{ service, jid, password, muc_service }`, but the plugin reads `username` + `domain` and has no `jid` key — and because backend_config is unvalidated, following DESIGN silently yields the default account.
failure: An operator writing `backend_config: { service: 'xmpp://host:5222', jid: 'bot@example.com', password: 's3cret', muc_service: 'muc.example.com' }` gets a bridge that ignores `jid` entirely, authenticates as username 'parley' on domain 'parley.local' with the supplied password, and fails SASL against a real server with no message pointing at the key. Neither `jid` nor `username`/`domain` is reconciled anywhere; packages/bridge-xmpp/README.md's config block is the correct one, so the two documents disagree.
remediation: Correct DESIGN.md line 477 to `{ service, domain, username, password, muc_service, nick?, mam_page? }` to match src/index.ts's XmppBackendConfig, and (with the unknown-key validation above) make a stray `jid` a named load error rather than a silent no-op.
testUpgrade: Class = "a config key documented in one place and unimplemented in the code". Add a test that reads the XmppBackendConfig interface's key set (or a single exported CONFIG_KEYS const) and asserts it matches the keys in the README's config block and the DESIGN §11 line, so any of the three drifting fails the build. Apply the same shape to every backend, since the DESIGN §11 line lists keys for all of them.

summary: `msgId` reads `this.incarnations` cache, which only `ensureStream`, `readRecent` and `subscribe`'s rebuild refresh. `post` never refreshes it, so a stream re-created out-of-band that `post` never observes as a 503 keeps minting the PREVIOUS incarnation's ids — and JetStream sequences restart at 1, so the ids collide exactly.
failure: Reproduced against a real `nats:2.10-alpine -js` container (port 4333): plugin.post(topic,'one') -> backendMsgId `20260729T214258092280859Z-1`; then out-of-band `jsm.streams.delete('PROBE_reprov1')` + `jsm.streams.add(...)` (an operator, or another Parley bridge's ensureStream, recreating it before our next publish, so our publish never sees the 503); then plugin.post(topic,'two') -> backendMsgId `20260729T214258092280859Z-1`, byte-identical. Core's SeenSet dedups on backendMsgId, so the genuinely-new second message is dropped on the floor. Also reproduced with the package's own fake by setting `streamCreated` to a new stamp with `publishMissing: 0`.
remediation: Make the incarnation a property of the observed publish, not of a cache that only some paths refresh: either re-read `streams.info` (and `noteIncarnation`) whenever `ensured` was memoized but the incarnation is older than the publish, or derive the id from something the PubAck itself carries (`ack.stream` + a per-connect nonce is not enough — prefer periodically revalidating `created`, or refreshing the incarnation on every `ensureStream` hit rather than only on a miss).
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a re-provisioned store must mint disjoint ids, for EVERY way the plugin can learn (or fail to learn) about the re-provision'. packages/bridge-nats/test/msg-id.test.ts already tables the three id minters but its single `reprovision()` helper always sets `publishMissing = 1`, hard-wiring the one recovery trigger. Turn the trigger into a second table axis — `{ observed: '503 on publish' }`, `{ observed: 'stream info re-read' }`, `{ observed: 'nothing — recreated between our calls' }` — and run all three minters against all three triggers; the third row fails today. Widen it further so the incarnation stamp is generated (not two fixed constants), so a fold that collapses stamps is caught too.

summary: The delivery-sequence gap check is guarded by `nextDelivery !== 0`, so the FIRST message a freshly-built consumer yields is never checked. With `AckPolicy.None` the server counts a message delivered the instant it writes it to the link, so if the consumer's very first delivery went into a link that then died while `consume()` reconnected transparently, the client's first observed `deliverySequence` is 2 and the hole is invisible — and `lastSeq` then jumps past the lost message, so no rebuild can recover it.
failure: Reproduced with the package's own fake (`fakeJetStream({ records: [], swallowed: [1] })`), the exact fixture subscribe-loop.test.ts uses: subscribe, publish seq 1..4, and `m1` is never delivered to the handler and never redelivered — the loop never rebuilds because `nextDelivery === 0` skipped the check on `m2` (deliverySequence 2). Rows `swallowed: [2] / [3] / [3,4] / [2,4]` all recover; `[1]` is silent permanent loss. The file's own comment claims 'Every position a hole can occupy is covered' — position 1 is not.
remediation: Initialise `nextDelivery = 1`: a newly created JetStream consumer's first delivery always has `deliverySequence === 1`, so the check is exact from the first message and needs no primed-state exemption. (Equivalently, keep the sentinel but treat `m.info.deliverySequence !== 1` on the first message as a gap.)
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a hole anywhere in the consumer's delivery sequence, INCLUDING at its very first delivery, must trigger a rebuild'. In packages/bridge-nats/test/subscribe-loop.test.ts, generate the `holes` table rather than hand-listing it: for a run of N messages, enumerate every non-empty subset of positions 1..N-1 (or a seeded random sample), so position 1 and multi-hole combinations are covered by construction and a future exemption for any position fails. Also drop the fake's `generation === 1` restriction on `swallowed` so a hole can be injected into a REBUILT consumer's first delivery too.

summary: The 18x3 `junkCursors` table branches on `if (outcome instanceof Error)` and otherwise only asserts `messages.length > 0` and `nextCursor !== junk` — both of which hold when the junk cursor is silently coerced to 'no since'. So all 54 cases pass whether the plugin rejects the cursor or silently ignores it: they cannot fail for the defect they are named after.
failure: Mutation: replaced the `throw` in `parseCursor` with `return undefined`. `npx vitest run packages/bridge-nats/test/cursor-input.test.ts` -> `2 failed | 68 passed`. All 54 junk-cursor table cases stayed green (a junk `since` becomes a no-since read returning all 3 messages with nextCursor '3'); only the two single-instance tests ('rejects the promise instead of throwing synchronously' and 'never reaches the server'), both hard-coded to `'abc'`, caught it. The class is pinned at exactly one input while 54 counted-as-coverage cases are inert.
remediation: Make the table assert the outcome unconditionally: every junk cursor must reject with /invalid nats cursor/ containing the offending value. If some inputs are deliberately acceptable, list them as an explicit `accepted: true` axis (the way config.test.ts does for prefixes) instead of an `if` that swallows either result.
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a validation table that branches on the result it is validating'. (a) Rewrite the junkCursors table as an outcome-pinned table (`{ value, rejected: true }`), and fold the two 'abc' one-offs into it as extra assertion axes so every input is checked for promise-rejection and for never-reaching-the-server. (b) Widen the generator: fuzz `since` over a character-class generator (unicode digits, whitespace-padded decimals, exponent/hex/bignum forms, empty) rather than a fixed 18-item list. (c) Sweep the package for the same shape — resource.test.ts's `outcome()` helper is a near-miss of the same pattern and should be audited.

summary: `want = min(limit, lastSeq - startSeq + 1)` over-counts a sparse range, and the loop's only early exits are `messages.length >= want` and `m.seq >= lastSeq`. When the hole is at the TAIL — `state.last_seq` names a deleted message — neither can ever fire, so every `fetchRecent` on that topic waits out the full `FETCH_EXPIRY_MS`. The condition is permanent until someone publishes again.
failure: Reproduced against a real `nats:2.10-alpine -js` (port 4333): post a,b,c to topic `tailhole`, then `jsm.streams.deleteMessage('P5_tailhole', 3)`. `streams.info` reports `{messages:2, first_seq:1, last_seq:3, num_deleted:1}`. `plugin.fetchRecent({topic})` returns `['a','b']` after **2010 ms** (the whole 2s expiry) instead of returning promptly, and repeats that 2s tax on every subsequent call, including `since:'2'` where `startSeq=3` yields nothing and `nextCursor` returns to '2'.
remediation: Stop the pull on the server's own view of the range rather than on `last_seq`: either bound the read by `info.state.messages` as well as by the sequence span, or add a short idle/no-message deadline to the fetch (e.g. close the batch after ~100-200 ms with no new message once at least the reachable window has been probed), so a hole anywhere — including the tail — ends the page instead of burning `expires`.
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'the sequence range is not dense — a page must return promptly for a hole in ANY position'. packages/bridge-nats/test/window.test.ts already tables six sparse shapes and asserts `elapsed < EXPIRY_MS/2`, but every shape's last element is present. Add a `tailGap` axis to the shape generator (e.g. `{ seqs, lastSeqOverride }`, and teach `fakeJetStream`'s `streams.info` to report a `last_seq` above the highest stored record), then cross it with the existing `positions` table. Better: generate `seqs` as a random subset of 1..N with `last_seq = N`, so tail, interior and front holes are all produced without being enumerated.

summary: `disconnect()` splices every registered closer out of `this.subscriptions`, but a subscribe loop parked in `await delay(RESUBSCRIBE_BACKOFF_MS)` (where an outage keeps it most of the time) does not re-check `live()` until after the delay. If `connect()` runs before it wakes, `this.stopped` is false and `nc` is live again, so the OLD loop rebuilds its consumer and keeps delivering to the OLD handler — with no closer registered, so no later `disconnect()` can close its iterator or delete its server-side consumer.
failure: Reproduced with the package's own fake: subscribe with `silentExits: 3` (loop cycling through the backoff), wait 1200 ms, `await plugin.disconnect()`, then re-apply exactly what `connect()` does (`stopped = false`, re-attach js/jsm/nc). `subscriptions.length` is 0, yet publishing `after-reconnect` still reaches the original handler ~3 s later. The connect()/disconnect() reuse cycle is explicitly supported — connect() clears `ensured`/`incarnations` and packages/bridge-nats/test/recovery.test.ts asserts it — so a caller that reconnects gets duplicate live delivery and an unstoppable loop.
remediation: Make the loop's identity generational: capture an epoch counter at `subscribe()` time (bumped by both `disconnect()` and `connect()`) and gate `live()` on `epoch === myEpoch`, so a loop whose epoch was retired exits regardless of what a later connect() does. Interrupting the backoff on disconnect (an abortable delay) is a worthwhile second half.
testUpgrade: CLASS = 'a background loop must be stoppable at every await point in its cycle, and must never resurrect'. Add a parameterized teardown-point table to packages/bridge-nats/test/subscribe-loop.test.ts: for each await the loop can be parked at (`RESUBSCRIBE_BACKOFF_MS` delay, `streamInfo`, `consumers.add`, `consume()`, mid-message-iteration), call `disconnect()` at that point, then run a `connect()` cycle, and assert (a) no message reaches the old handler and (b) `fake.state.created` stops growing. Parameterize the pause offset over a sweep of delays so the timing window is covered rather than one lucky value.

summary: `http()` never passes `deadlineMs`, so every `/api/v1/events` long-poll inherits net-util's `DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS` (30s). Any `events_timeout_ms` above ~30000 — a range `connect()` accepts and the README documents as valid ([250, 600000]) — is severed by the shared deadline before the plugin's own cap fires, and because `capped` is false the loop treats a healthy idle poll as a failure: `backoff()` → `degrade()` → escalating waits and `console.error` spam. `bridge-matrix` fixes exactly this with `syncDeadlineMs(timeout)` (src/index.ts:505/542/650) and a dedicated test; Zulip has neither. The blocking-fetch `pollForWake` has the same shape: core passes `blockMs` up to `catchup.block_max_ms` (60000), so a 60s wait is cut at 30s and re-arms a fresh dedicated queue.
failure: connect({ events_timeout_ms: 35000 }) + subscribe on an idle topic (server heartbeat 120s). Expected: one parked long-poll for 35s. Actual (reproduced): 2 polls in 33s — the first aborts at 30s with net-util's `→ deadline: no response within 30000ms`, `capped === false`, so the loop calls `backoff('events long-poll failed')`, decrements `healthy` (blocking fetchRecent stops piggybacking and opens dedicated queues instead), and after 3 idle cycles logs `[parley-zulip] push loop for topic "…" has failed 3× in a row` — a permanently-failing loop report for a perfectly healthy server.
remediation: Pass an explicit `deadlineMs` on every request that is expected to park: `this.eventsTimeoutMs + DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS` for the subscribe loop's `/events` poll, and `(deadline - Date.now()) + DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS` for `pollForWake`. Mirror `bridge-matrix`'s `syncDeadlineMs`. Either that, or lower `MAX_EVENTS_TIMEOUT_MS` below `DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS` and correct the README — but the blocking-fetch path still needs the raise, since `block_max_ms` defaults to 60000.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "a request the plugin intends to block longer than the shared default deadline must raise `deadlineMs`", not the 35000 instance. Two layers: (1) a spy/mock over `fetchWithRetry` (copy `packages/bridge-matrix/test/sync-deadline.fake.test.ts`) asserting, for a table of `events_timeout_ms` values crossing DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS — [250, 25000, 30000, 30001, 60000, 600000] — that the `/events` call's `deadlineMs >= events_timeout_ms + DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS`, and that `pollForWake`'s `deadlineMs >= blockMs`, while every non-long-poll route leaves it undefined; (2) widen the existing `config.test.ts` CONFIG_ROWS `events_timeout_ms` rows past 30000 and strengthen "runs a sane loop" to also assert zero `console.error` and that the poll count over an idle window equals ceil(window / events_timeout_ms) — the current row (`Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, 800ms window, `< 20` requests) cannot distinguish a 600s cap from a 30s one.

summary: `zulipToMessage` trusts the wire types it declares. `m.timestamp` goes straight into `new Date(x * 1000).toISOString()`, which throws RangeError for anything non-finite or past Date's ±8.64e15 range, and `m.content ?? ''` passes a non-string through to core's `parseMentions`, which calls `.matchAll` on it. Either throw escapes `fetchRecent` (and `gapFill`), so one poisoned record bricks catch-up on every restart. `bridge-matrix` guards this exact class with `MAX_TIMESTAMP_MS` + `typeof body === 'string'` (src/index.ts:977-998) and `bridge-redis` with `entryTimestamp` (src/index.ts:729-734); Zulip guards only `undefined`.
failure: A server answering `GET /api/v1/messages` with `{result:'success',messages:[{id:7,content:'x',sender_email:'a@b',timestamp:1e18}]}` → `fetchRecent` rejects with `RangeError: Invalid time value` at src/index.ts:932. Same for `timestamp:'nope'`. With `{...,content:42,timestamp:1}` → `TypeError: content.matchAll is not a function` from `parseMentions`. All three reproduced against a minimal hostile http server; the plugin has no path that recovers, so catch-up fails identically on every subsequent start.
remediation: Coerce every field a server controls before it reaches `buildMessage`: an `isoTimestamp(ts: unknown)` helper bounded by ±8.64e15 falling back to epoch (lift Matrix's, or move it into `parley-net-util` so the five HTTP backends share one), `typeof m.content === 'string' ? m.content : ''`, `typeof m.sender_email === 'string' ? … : ''`, and reject/skip a record whose `id` is not a finite integer rather than minting the cursor `'undefined'`/`NaN`.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "no server-controlled field shape can throw out of the seam" with a parameterized hostile-payload table shared across the HTTP backends, driven by a generator over each field × {missing, null, wrong type, empty string, 0, negative, 1e18, -1e18, NaN, Infinity, huge string, non-ASCII}: for every combination assert `fetchRecent` resolves, the returned `Message` is well-formed (string timestamp parseable by `Date.parse`, string content, non-empty backendMsgId), and — the half that matters here — that a `subscribe` handler receiving the same payload leaves the loop alive and produces no unhandled rejection. No existing zulip test ever feeds the plugin a payload the fake did not construct, which is why the whole class is invisible today.

summary: The subscribe loop's error containment covers only `handler(m)` (inside `deliver`) and the HTTP/gap-fill awaits. Anything else that throws inside `loop()` — notably `zulipToMessage(topic, ev.message)` at line 701, evaluated *before* `deliver` is entered — rejects `loop()`. `const running = loop().finally(...)` and `void running.finally(() => this.loopExits.delete(running))` each derive a promise that rejects with no handler; `Promise.allSettled(exits)` in `disconnect()` handles `running` itself but not the `void`-ed derivative. On Node 22 (`--unhandled-rejections=throw` by default) that is an uncaught exception, and `src/cli.ts` installs no `uncaughtException`/`unhandledRejection` handler, so the MCP stdio server dies. It also silently kills push for every other topic in the process.
failure: A `GET /api/v1/events` response `{result:'success',events:[{id:0,type:'message',message:{id:5,content:'hi',sender_email:'a@b',timestamp:1e18}}]}` after a normal subscribe handshake. Reproduced: `process.on('unhandledRejection')` fires with `[RangeError: Invalid time value]`, the loop is gone (no further polls), and no `console.error` names the backend — under `parley-zulip` the process would have exited instead.
remediation: Wrap the whole `while (alive())` body (or at minimum the event-drain `for` loop) in a try/catch that routes an unexpected throw through `backoff(...)` so it is paced and reported, and attach a terminal `.catch()` to `running`/its derivatives so no exit path can produce an unhandled rejection. Normalizing the payload (previous finding) removes today's trigger; this removes the class.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "no throw anywhere inside the push loop can escape as an unhandled rejection or silently end push", parameterized over injected fault sites rather than one payload: for each of {a poisoned message event, a handler that throws, a `wake()` that throws, a malformed non-message event, an events response that is valid JSON of the wrong shape}, install a `process.on('unhandledRejection')` collector, assert it stays empty, assert `console.error` named `[parley-zulip]`, and assert the loop still delivers a subsequently posted message. The existing lifecycle/operability tables only ever inject *transport* faults (status codes, hangs, GCs), so every non-transport throw site is ungraded.

summary: The `resolveIdentity` table grades the active-member filter only on the `full_name` branch ('a deactivated member is not a match' uses the name 'Gone Away'). Nothing resolves a deactivated member's *email*, so the `active` filter on the email path is untested — the docstring at src/index.ts:720-724 claims deactivated matches degrade for both, but only half is guarded.
failure: Mutation `const byEmail = active.find(...)` → `members.find(...)` in src/index.ts:734 leaves the entire package suite green (74 passed / 1 skipped across server-constraints + conformance). A deactivated account's email would then resolve to its stale `user_id` with no test noticing, which is precisely the aliasing the surrounding code exists to prevent.
remediation: No source change needed — the code is correct. Add the missing row.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "every resolution branch is graded against every directory hazard" by turning the table into a cross-product of {handle is an email, handle is a full_name} × {unique active, duplicated across two active members, only match deactivated, match deactivated + a distinct active one, no match} and asserting the expected backendRef for each cell — so a later reviewer meeting this theme on a new branch (a `delivery_email` field, a bot-vs-human filter) finds the shape already parameterized. Add 'gone@example.com' → 'gone@example.com' as the cell that fails against the mutation above.

summary: `wireTopic` deliberately counts code points (`[...wire].length`) because Zulip truncates by Python character, and case-folds with JS `toLowerCase()` which can change a string's length. Both the length table ('a'.repeat(n)) and the case-folding table ('ops'/'OPS', 'Alpha'/'alpha', …) are 100% ASCII/BMP, so neither distinction is graded anywhere in the package.
failure: Mutation `[...wire].length` → `wire.length` (UTF-16 units) in src/index.ts:753/755 leaves the suite green. Under that mutation a legal 40-emoji topic (80 UTF-16 units) is wrongly rejected with 'Zulip topic too long: 80 characters', and a 60-code-point topic containing astral characters becomes unusable — a silent namespace regression that the current tables cannot see. The lowercase-expansion direction (e.g. U+0130 'İ' → 2 code points, so a 60-character topic can cross the wire limit only after folding) is likewise ungraded.
remediation: No source change needed. Widen the tables so the code-point choice is load-bearing.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "the topic mapping is graded in code points, not UTF-16 units, and across the case-folding edge" by parameterizing both tables over a character-set axis — [ASCII, Latin-1 accented, CJK, astral emoji, a combining sequence, U+0130/U+0131, U+00DF] × lengths [1, max-1, max, max+1] — asserting round-trip equality below the cap, rejection naming the count above it, and that the reported count equals `[...name].length`; and add case-collision rows in a non-ASCII script so 'a third party posting a case variant lands in the SAME Parley topic' is checked where JS folding and the server's folding can actually disagree.

summary: `requireNonEmpty` embeds the offending value in its message, and `connect()` calls it for `api_key`. A key that fails the string test — e.g. a YAML `api_key: 1234567890` read as a number — is echoed verbatim into the thrown message, which `src/cli.ts:53-56` writes to stderr as `err.stack`, and which core surfaces as an `isError` tool result (i.e. model context). Every other credential-bearing path in the repo redacts: net-util's `redactUrls` exists specifically so 'a credential-bearing URL never reaches model context or the operator's logs'.
failure: `connect({ site_url: 'https://z.example.com', email: 'bot@x', api_key: 1234567890 })` throws `backend_config.api_key must be a non-empty string (got 1234567890)`; `parley-zulip: fatal: …` then prints the secret to stderr. The same happens for any non-string secret shape (a nested object stringified by `JSON.stringify`).
remediation: Give `requireNonEmpty` a `secret` flag (or a sibling `requireNonEmptySecret`) that reports only the offending *type* and length — `backend_config.api_key must be a non-empty string (got number)` — and use it for `api_key`. Keep the value echo for non-secret keys (`stream`, `site_url`) where it is the useful diagnostic.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "no validation, warning or error message ever contains a configured secret" with a parameterized case over every secret-bearing key × every rejected shape (number, null, empty string, whitespace, object, array, boolean): connect with a sentinel value, capture the rejection message plus everything written to `console.warn`/`console.error`, and assert the sentinel appears in none of them while the key name appears in all. Point it at the config surface generically so a future `backend_config` secret (a webhook token, a client secret) is covered the day it is added; the existing config.test.ts asserts only `rejects.toThrow(row.key)`, which passes whether or not the value leaks.

summary: CLAUDE.md restricts comments to risk warnings phrased 'keep X, so that Y' and puts justification, alternatives and reviewer-facing reasoning in the commit message. Several comments here are argument rather than warning, and the package's own `comment-hygiene.test.ts` lint (tracker IDs, issue refs, four phrase patterns, 'reviewer') cannot see the shape — so the rule is enforced only where it is cheapest to satisfy.
failure: src/index.ts:320-323 restates the `if` on line 324 and then argues its safety to a reader ('Returning early/empty stays safe — core's generic wrapper polls the remaining budget — so this only ever SHORTENS the wait'); line 60 narrates a design choice ('`queueId` is mutable because a GC'd queue is re-registered'); the class JSDoc at 117-141 carries ~25 lines of design prose (the ONE INEXACTNESS section) duplicated almost verbatim in README.md:55-63, where it can rot independently. None of the four BANNED patterns matches any of them, so the lint reports clean.
remediation: Delete the fetchRecent block comment (the condition `messages.length === 0 && args.since !== undefined && (args.blockMs ?? 0) > 0` already states it; the safety argument belongs in the commit that introduced it) and the line-60 narration. Keep the mutable-topics warning in exactly one place — README — and have the JSDoc point at it rather than restate it.
testUpgrade: Guard the class "a source comment warns about a risk; it does not justify, narrate or duplicate prose" by widening `comment-hygiene.test.ts` beyond phrase blacklists: add checks that flag a comment restating an identifier from the next non-comment line, a block comment longer than N lines outside a JSDoc, a comment containing a first-person-plural justification ('so this only ever', 'stays safe', 'is safe because', 'because a … is'), and any run of ≥3 words duplicated between src/**.ts comments and the package README. Assert the widened lint fails against the three sites above before it is committed.

summary: The IDENTIFY backoff ladder is sized for exactly one dialer per bot token, but the README tells operators to share one token across every bridge instance — so N instances flapping together blow the 1000/24h quota and Discord resets the token.
failure: RECONNECT_CAP_MS is 120_000 and its own JSDoc justifies it as "ABOVE 86.4s" (= 86400s/1000), i.e. one dial per 86.4s is the whole per-token budget. Steady state per instance is therefore ~30 dials/h = ~720 IDENTIFY/day; I measured 34–36 sockets/h for a single long-polling instance against a broken gateway (instrumented gateway-budget table). README "Multiple concurrent sessions" says "Any number of bridge instances — one per Claude Code session plus the remote/chat server — may share a single bot ... each instance holds its own gateway socket." Concrete input: two Code sessions + one remote bridge on one shared bot token, gateway flapping for 24h → 3 × 720 = 2160 IDENTIFYs against a 1000/24h quota → Discord RESETS the bot token, killing every Parley instance on it until a human re-provisions. The suite's own invariant is asserted per-process (`totalIdentifies() * 24 < 1000` in gateway-budget.test.ts:140), so it can never see this.
remediation: Either size the ladder for the documented fan-out (cap = 86.4s × expected_instances, or make the cap configurable with a documented per-token divisor), or stop recommending a shared token for push-enabled instances: state in the README that the 1000/24h IDENTIFY quota is per bot token and that a shared token must be reactive-only (`live_push.enabled: false`, no `block_ms` long-poll, so nothing dials the gateway). Whichever is chosen, the README's quota claim and the RECONNECT_CAP_MS JSDoc must name the number of concurrent dialers they assume.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a per-account rate/quota budget asserted against one process": parameterize the existing gateway-budget table over an `instances` dimension (1, 2, 4) that stands up N DiscordPlugin objects sharing one token against the same fake gateway, and assert `sum(totalIdentifies over all instances) * (DAY_MS/HOUR_MS) < QUOTA_PER_DAY`. gateway-budget.test.ts:140 is too narrow because it counts one plugin. The same generator shape should be reused for any vendor quota that is keyed by credential rather than by process (Slack/Telegram rate buckets).

summary: Nothing in 194 tests asserts what the IDENTIFY frame or the REST request actually carries: dropping the MESSAGE_CONTENT intent bit, blanking the bot token, and deleting the `Authorization: Bot` header all leave the whole suite green.
failure: Three separate mutations of packages/bridge-discord/src/index.ts, each run against the full package suite: (1) `const INTENTS = (1 << 0) | (1 << 9);` (MESSAGE_CONTENT 1<<15 removed) → 194 passed; (2) `token: ''` in the IDENTIFY payload → 194 passed; (3) deleting `if (this.token !== undefined) headers.Authorization = \`Bot ${this.token}\`;` → 194 passed. In production each is fatal and silent-ish: (1) every MESSAGE_CREATE arrives with empty `content`, which is exactly the failure the README's provisioning step 2 exists to prevent, and the plugin would push empty-bodied messages into the session; (2)/(3) Discord answers 401 / closes 4004, and the plugin's own terminal handling then marks the gateway permanently fatal. fake-gateway.ts only records op-2 frames (`identified()`, `heartbeatsSent()`) and never inspects `frame.d`; fake-discord.ts never reads `req.headers.authorization`.
remediation: Make both fakes enforce the wire contract rather than merely log it: fake-gateway's op-2 branch should reject (serverClose(4004)) unless `d.token` equals the configured token, and close 4014 unless `d.intents & (1<<15)` is set; fake-discord should answer `401 {code: 0}` to any request whose `Authorization` is not `Bot <token>`. Then add one assertion on the decoded IDENTIFY payload (token, intents bitfield) so the bit that gates message content is pinned by value.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a fake that accepts requests it should refuse": add a table over required wire facts — [`Authorization: Bot <token>` on every REST path, `d.token` on IDENTIFY, each required intent bit] × [present → succeeds, absent/wrong → the vendor's real rejection] driven through the fakes, so any future plugin change that stops sending one loses a test. Parameterize the intent bits from an exported `REQUIRED_INTENTS` list rather than the packed constant, so a later added intent joins the table by construction.

summary: A transient gateway close on the FIRST dial schedules no reconnect at all — the plugin that has a 120s-capped reconnect ladder for every later outage has zero in-plugin recovery for the outage most likely at process start, and `subscribe` rejecting kills the whole bridge process.
failure: Probe (fake `ws`, fake timers): `state.onIdentify = ws => ws.serverClose(1006)`, then `connect()` + `subscribe('880009')`. subscribe rejects with `Error: Discord gateway closed before READY (code 1006)`. The close handler's reconnect branch is `else if (ready)` — `ready` is false, so `scheduleReconnect` is never called; the probe then let the gateway recover and advanced 10 simulated minutes: sockets opened stayed at 1 and `vi.getTimerCount()` was 0. The rejection is not a NoSuchTopicError, so bridge-core's startPushLoop (push-loop.ts:47) rethrows, stdio-bridge's attach tears the bridge down, and cli.ts exits 1 — so a one-second gateway blip at launch takes down the reactive half (post/fetch_recent) too, which needs no gateway. The gateway-budget suite's three `subscribe` rows pass through this path and never notice, because they only assert an upper bound.
remediation: Have the first dial join the same recovery loop every later one uses: on a non-terminal close/handshake failure with `ready === false`, call `scheduleReconnect(url, epoch)` (the epoch guard and `chargeDialAttempt` already pace it, so the quota argument is unchanged) and let `subscribe` resolve optimistically once the dial has been scheduled — the gateway only ever delivers new messages and catch-up owns history, so a subscription that goes live a backoff later loses nothing. Keep a terminal close rejecting, since that genuinely needs a human.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a recovery loop that only covers the steady state": parameterize a reconnect table over WHEN the failure lands — [first dial, mid-handshake, after READY, mid-reconnect] × [transient close, handshake stall, terminal close] — asserting for every transient cell that the plugin re-dials on its own within a bounded number of ladder steps AND that live push resumes once the gateway recovers. Replace `expect(instances.length).toBeLessThanOrEqual(MAX_SOCKETS_PER_HOUR)` in gateway-budget.test.ts:139 with a two-sided band (`>= 1` retry and `<= ceiling`), so a cell can no longer pass by never retrying.

summary: Three of the nine IDENTIFY-budget cells (every `subscribe` initiator row) are satisfied by the plugin dialing exactly once in a simulated hour, so they cost seconds and discriminate nothing.
failure: Instrumented the table to print its own measurements: `subscribe | close before HELLO → sockets=1 identifies=0`, `subscribe | close after IDENTIFY (4008) → sockets=1 identifies=1`, `subscribe | handshake stalls → sockets=1 identifies=1`. Against `MAX_SOCKETS_PER_HOUR = 42` and `totalIdentifies() * 24 < 1000`, all three pass with a margin of ~40x — and would still pass if the backoff ladder, `chargeDialAttempt`, and `nextDialAt` were deleted outright, because nothing in those rows re-dials. The only rows that exercise the ladder are the ones driven by core's 250 ms long-poll fallback.
remediation: Give the assertion a lower bound as well as an upper one (a transient-failure cell must dial at least twice, i.e. the ladder actually ran), or drop the `subscribe`-only rows and keep the long-poll ones, which are the cells that exercise the budget. Fixing finding #3 makes the lower bound meaningful for all nine cells.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a rate/budget assertion with only a ceiling": express every budget case as a band — `expect(dials).toBeGreaterThan(1)` and `expect(dials * scale).toBeLessThan(quota)` — and derive the band from the exported ladder constants so a cell whose driver does nothing fails the floor instead of passing the ceiling.

summary: Two deliberate state resets are unguarded: deleting `this.subs.clear()` from disconnect() and deleting the negative-cache reset in resolveIdentity both leave all 194 tests green, even though each protects a real behaviour.
failure: Mutation 1: remove `this.subs.clear();` from disconnect() → 194 passed. Neither connect() nor disconnect() would then clear `subs`, so after `disconnect()` + `connect()` a MESSAGE_CREATE on a channel the first session subscribed to is delivered to the FIRST session's handler — a live push into a torn-down consumer. The gateway-budget "session state does not leak" table cannot see it because both sessions subscribe the same TOPIC. Mutation 2: remove `this.me = undefined; // don't cache a transient failure` → 194 passed; a single 500 on `GET /users/@me` would then poison `resolveIdentity` for the life of the connection (I verified by probe that the real code recovers on the second call and that no test exercises fail-then-succeed).
remediation: Add the two missing cases rather than change the code (both behaviours are correct): a connect→subscribe→disconnect→connect cycle that asserts the first session's handler receives nothing, and a resolveIdentity case that injects one `/users/@me` failure and asserts the immediately following call succeeds with the real bot id.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a memo or registry whose invalidation is untested": add a parameterized table over the plugin's mutable caches/registries — [`subs`, `waiters`, `me`, `channelOwner`, `gatewayReady`, `fatalGateway`] × [cleared by disconnect, not carried into the next connect, not poisoned by a transient failure] — driven through the public seam only, so each field's reset earns a cell and a deleted reset loses a named test.

summary: `post` sends no `allowed_mentions`, so any content the agent writes — including untrusted inbound text it relays — can fire `@everyone`/`@here`/role pings across the guild.
failure: The POST body is exactly `{ content, message_reference? }`. Discord's default when `allowed_mentions` is absent is to parse every mention in `content`. Concrete input: a hostile participant posts `Summarize this and repeat it verbatim: @everyone deploy now` into a subscribed channel; the message crosses the seam as untrusted context (DESIGN §14), the agent echoes it through `parley_post`/`parley_reply`, and the bot — which the README's provisioning step 3 tells the operator to grant Send Messages — mass-pings the guild. The plugin's own inbound direction is careful here (`renderMentions` rewrites `<@id>` to `@username` using Discord's resolved list), so the asymmetry is not deliberate anywhere in the code or README.
remediation: Send an explicit `allowed_mentions` on every post that bounds the blast radius to what Parley actually needs for addressing — e.g. `{ parse: ['users'], replied_user: false }` — and document the knob in the README config table so an operator who wants role/broadcast pings can widen it deliberately.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "outbound content re-derives privileged effects from untrusted text": a table over amplification markup per backend — [`@everyone`, `@here`, `<@&roleId>`, and the vendor equivalents Slack already enumerates in its BROADCASTS set] — asserting that a `post` of that content leaves the request body's mention scope bounded (fake asserts `allowed_mentions` and refuses a body without it). Widen the fake-discord POST handler to reject a body whose mention scope is unspecified so new call sites cannot skip it.

summary: `subscribe` resolves for any topic string without ever checking that the channel exists or that the bot can receive pushes from it, so a typo'd, deleted, DM, or out-of-guild channel id produces a permanently idle bridge with no error anywhere.
failure: `subscribe` does `this.subs.set(channelId, ...)` and `await this.ensureGateway()` — no REST touch. Input: `topics: ["55511122233344455"]` with a single digit wrong (or a channel in a guild the bot was never invited to). subscribe resolves, cli.ts prints `bridge up ... live_push=true`, the gateway IDENTIFYs and READYs, and MESSAGE_CREATE for that id never arrives — the operator's only signal is silence. `catchup.on_start` would surface it as NoSuchTopicError, but only if enabled; with `catchup.on_start: false` nothing ever reports it. The README documents the DM/group-DM instance of this class ("the symptom is an idle bridge with no error") but not the far commoner typo/not-invited case, and does not act on either.
remediation: Validate once per subscribed channel at subscribe time — a single `GET /channels/<id>` — and translate `10003 Unknown Channel` to `NoSuchTopicError` (which core's push loop already handles by skipping the topic with a diagnostic) and `50001 Missing Access` / a non-guild channel `type` into a thrown error naming the channel and the reason. That is one cheap request per topic at startup and turns every member of this class from silence into a line on stderr.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "subscribe accepts a topic it can never deliver": a table over unreachable channel classes — [never created (10003), exists but no access (50001), DM channel `type: 1`, group DM `type: 3`] × [subscribe outcome, whether a diagnostic naming the channel was written] — with the fake serving each class, so any future channel class that cannot push must be classified explicitly instead of resolving silently.

summary: `openSocket`'s close handler infers "was this pre-`hello`?" from whether *this* call settled the handshake promise. A handshake timeout or a websocket `error` settles it FIRST, so the ensuing `close` is misread as a post-`hello` drop and calls `void this.reconnect()`. Each new reconnect owner immediately dials again, and each of its failures spawns another owner — the loops multiply geometrically and never stop, bypassing `dialCooldownUntil` entirely (which only guards `ensurePollSocket`, not `reconnect`).
failure: Reproduced in-worktree. (a) `apps.connections.open` returns a websocket URL that refuses connection (ws://127.0.0.1:1 — the everyday shape: firewall/proxy/blip). One `subscribe()` rejects with ECONNREFUSED, and 3 s later the plugin has issued **2729 `apps.connections.open` dials** with **1299 live reconnect owners**, growing ~1000 dials/second forever — against Slack's tightest-limit endpoint, guaranteeing app-level throttling/disablement, from a caller that already gave up. (b) A Socket Mode edge that accepts the TCP connection and stays silent (`handshake_timeout_ms: 150`): 27 dials / 26 owners after 4 s, forever. By contrast the immediate `pre-hello-close` shape (the one the suite tests) correctly yields exactly 1 owner, because there `settle()` happens inside the close handler. This also falsifies README lines 61-63 ("the long-poll path backs off before dialling `apps.connections.open` again, so a core poll loop cannot turn one `fetch_recent` into hundreds of handshakes").
remediation: Stop deriving liveness from `settle()`'s return value. Keep an explicit per-connection `helloSeen` boolean, set only in `routeEnvelope`'s `hello` branch, and gate `void this.reconnect()` on it. Additionally make `reconnect()` single-owner (a `reconnecting` flag cleared in a `finally`), and route `reconnect`'s dials through the same cooldown as `ensurePollSocket` so an outage costs O(elapsed/backoff) dials no matter how many entry points observe it.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the existing conformance case `repeated pre-`hello` closes keep exactly one reconnect owner` over the FAILURE SHAPE rather than one shape: {`apps.connections.open` ok:false, immediate pre-`hello` close, silent socket → handshake timeout, unroutable ws URL → connect error, post-`hello` drop} × {entry point: subscribe, blocking fetchRecent}. For every row assert (i) reconnect owners ≤ 1 and (ii) `apps.connections.open` dials ≤ ceil(elapsedMs/DIAL_BACKOFF_MS)+1 measured over ≥2 s of sustained outage. Add `GreetMode` 'silent' and a 'dead-url' mode to `FakeSlack` so the generator covers shapes nobody enumerated.

summary: `mentionMap[id]` and `channelMap[topic]` index plain object literals with attacker- or caller-supplied keys, so `Object.prototype` members answer as if they were configured entries. `bridge-core` already guards exactly this class in `engine/read-state.ts` (`Object.create(null)`, with a `__proto__`/`constructor` test); the Slack plugin is the unguarded twin — and here one side of it (`mentionMap`) is reachable straight from untrusted inbound message text with no config prerequisite.
failure: Reproduced. (1) An inbound Slack message `hi <@constructor> and <@__proto__> and <@toString>` normalizes to content `hi @function Object() { [native code] } and @[object Object] and @function toString() { [native code] }` with `mentions: ["function"]` — vendor/attacker-controlled text injects JS engine internals into agent context and mints a mention handle present in no map. (2) `subscribe(asTopic('__proto__'))` RESOLVES successfully and then silently delivers nothing forever: `channelMap['__proto__']` is `Object.prototype`, so `routes` is keyed by an object that no string `event.channel` can ever match — a silent no-op, not a fail-fast. (3) `post(asTopic('constructor'))` against a channel literally named `constructor` that EXISTS rejects with `NoSuchTopicError` ("topic not present yet"), because `JSON.stringify(Object)` is `undefined` and the form field becomes the string "undefined". `topics`/`post_topics` in core are `z.string().min(1)`, so all three keys are legal config/tool inputs.
remediation: Build both maps as null-prototype objects at `connect()` (`Object.assign(Object.create(null), cfg.mention_map ?? {})`), or gate every lookup with `Object.hasOwn(map, key)`. Separately, make `channelFor` reject a resolved channel that is not a non-empty string, so a mapping fault can never degrade into a silent route miss or a false `NoSuchTopicError`.
testUpgrade: One parameterized table over META_KEYS = ['__proto__','constructor','prototype','toString','valueOf','hasOwnProperty'] crossed with each lookup site: as a `mention` body on BOTH delivery paths (assert content is byte-identical to the input markup and `mentions` is empty), and as a `topic` through all four seam entry points (`post`, `fetchRecent`, `fetchRecent-since`, `subscribe`) asserting the channel-id literal is used verbatim and a subscribed message is actually delivered. Mirror `bridge-core/src/engine/read-state.test.ts`'s prototype case so the class is guarded at both layers.

summary: `channelFor` claims channel ownership first-come-first-served from whichever topic happens to be resolved first, and the claim survives until `disconnect()`. Configuration is not privileged over an ad-hoc caller-supplied topic, so a single `post`/`fetch_recent` naming a channel-id literal can permanently take a *configured* topic's channel and disable it for the process lifetime.
failure: Reproduced. `channel_map: { 'ctx-payments': 'C0PAY' }`. An agent-driven `post(topic='C0PAY', ...)` (admitted by any `post_topics` pattern covering raw channel ids — the documented ad-hoc-posting use case, DESIGN §14) succeeds and claims C0PAY for topic "C0PAY". Every subsequent `post`/`fetchRecent`/`subscribe` on the configured topic `ctx-payments` then throws `Slack topics "C0PAY" and "ctx-payments" both resolve to channel C0PAY`. The bridge's primary topic is dead until restart, and the trigger can be steered by prompt-injected inbound content (DESIGN §14 "inbound is untrusted").
remediation: Seed `channelOwner` from `channel_map` inside `connect()` so configured topics own their channels before any call arrives, and treat an unmapped literal that collides with an already-owned channel as the rejected side. That keeps the collision fail-fast while making it impossible for a caller-supplied topic to displace a configured one.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the existing `hostile-input.test.ts` ENTRY_POINTS matrix over WHICH SIDE claims first: for every (first, second) pair also assert that when `first` is the unmapped literal and `second` is the *mapped* topic, it is the LITERAL that is rejected and the mapped topic keeps working — i.e. the configured side is never the loser. Widen to a third dimension (claimant = mapped | literal | presence topic).

summary: The waiter wake predicate `compareTs(event.ts, waiter.since) > 0` — the only thing that keeps a parked long-poll from waking on a message it has already seen — has no test that can fail on its removal. Mutation: delete the condition so every surfaced event wakes every waiter on that channel. All 262 tests in `packages/bridge-slack` stay green.
failure: Mutated `if (compareTs(event.ts, waiter.since) > 0) waiter.wake();` → `waiter.wake();` and ran `npx vitest run packages/bridge-slack`: 11 files / 262 tests passed. The class the guard protects is reachable: with two concurrent `parley_fetch_recent({topic, since, block_ms})` calls on one channel at different floors (A old, B new — legal, `since` is a caller argument), a message between A and B wakes B, whose exclusive re-query returns nothing, so B returns an empty page immediately instead of holding its budget. `block_ms` then degrades into the busy-return loop it exists to eliminate, and the token-cost claim in README lines 71-75 stops holding.
remediation: No source change needed for the guard itself; close the coverage hole. While there, note the channel-keying half of the predicate (`this.waiters.get(event.channel)`) is equally untested — a mutation to a single shared waiter key would also survive.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized `blocking-fetch` case over WAKE-ELIGIBILITY rather than wake-timing: rows = {event strictly above the floor, event exactly at the floor, event below the floor, event on a DIFFERENT channel}. Above-floor must resolve in ≪ blockMs; the other three must stay parked for ≥ 0.8·blockMs and return an empty page whose `nextCursor === since`. Drive two concurrent blocked fetches at different floors in one row so cross-waiter wakes are caught too.

summary: When the Socket Mode handshake is unavailable, `fetchRecent({blockMs})` gives up on the native wait and returns its (empty) first page at once. Core's generic wrapper then re-drives it every `block_poll_interval_ms`, so a single blocked `parley_fetch_recent` issues one `conversations.history` request per 250 ms for the entire `block_max_ms` budget. The dial cooldown bounds the *handshake* calls but nothing bounds the *history* calls.
failure: Measured with the shipped fake: `fetchRecentBlocking(plugin, {topic, since:'0'}, {blockMs:5000, pollIntervalMs:250})` with `apps.connections.open` failing issues **21 `conversations.history` requests in 5 s** → ~250 per default 60 s `block_max_ms`. `conversations.history` is a tiered, comparatively tight Slack method; ~250 calls/minute on one channel will 429, and each 429 whose `Retry-After` exceeds `DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS` (30 s) makes the call reject with `upstream asked for …, past this call's deadline` — so the long-poll fails outright and the channel's remaining budget is spent, starving `post`. README lines 61-63 describe this state as "catch-up continues over HTTP in the meantime", which understates it.
remediation: When the socket is unavailable, park the plugin call on a timer for the caller's `blockMs` (waking early if the socket recovers) and re-query once at the end, instead of returning immediately and inviting core to re-drive. That collapses ~250 history calls per blocked fetch to 2 while preserving the same observable contract.
testUpgrade: Widen the existing `handshake storm bound` table from one bounded resource to all of them: for each (blockMs, pollIntervalMs) row assert BOTH `hits('apps.connections.open')` and `hits('conversations.history')` are O(wall clock), e.g. ≤ ceil(blockMs/1000)+2 — a single bound parameterized over the method name, so a future path that trades one storm for another cannot pass.

summary: CLAUDE.md permits a comment only when it warns a future developer off a risky action, phrased "keep X, so that Y"; most comments here comply, but several are pure narration of the line below and should be deleted or replaced by clearer code. Notably, one of them sits exactly where the round's worst bug lives — the close handler is commented as if the `wasPreHello` branch were self-evidently correct, which is precisely the reading that hid the misclassification.
failure: `src/index.ts:581` `// Post-establishment errors surface as a close → the reconnect path below.` (narration, and factually the assumption that is wrong — a pre-`hello` `error` also surfaces as a close and takes that path); `:594` `// Post-'hello' close: this connection was live; mint a fresh single-use URL.` (restates the branch, and mislabels it — the branch is entered for handshake timeouts too); `:651` `// Slack is rotating this connection out; close → the 'close' handler reconnects fresh.` (narration); `:702` `// Slack form convention: scalar → string; array/object arg → JSON.stringify(value).` (restates the ternary below).
remediation: Replace the close-handler narration with the code the comments are standing in for: an explicit `helloSeen` flag (see the reconnect-storm finding) makes the two branches self-describing and removes the need for prose that can — and did — drift from the control flow. Delete the `disconnect`-envelope and form-encoding narration; the risk-phrased `// Socket Mode URLs are SINGLE-USE` and `// Keep the ack FIRST` comments are the shape to keep.
testUpgrade: Not a test-shaped class, but it is mechanically checkable: extend `bridge-core/src/source-hygiene.test.ts` to flag comment lines in `packages/*/src/**` that neither start with an imperative risk phrase (`Keep `, `Never `, `IMPORTANT`, `so that`) nor are a `/** */` doc block, and run it across every plugin so the rule is enforced uniformly instead of per-reviewer.

summary: `canonicalChatId` treats any string matching `/^-?\d+$/` as already canonical and returns it verbatim with no network call, but Telegram normalizes the number. A chat id written with leading zeros (or any spelling that is numerically but not textually canonical) makes the plugin key the store, the subscription and the fetch under the literal string while inbound updates and its own sendMessage response are keyed under Telegram's normalized id — so the topic is a permanent black hole, which is exactly what the function's own JSDoc claims it prevents.
failure: `plugin.post(asTopic('-0012345'), me, 'hello')` resolves with backendMsgId `-12345:1` (Telegram/fake stamped chat.id -12345) and `plugin.fetchRecent({topic: asTopic('-0012345')})` returns `{messages: [], nextCursor: '0'}` — forever, on every restart. Same for `'0012345'`. subscribe on that topic never fires. Because own posts never arrive via getUpdates and the Bot API has no history endpoint, those messages are unrecoverable. Confirmed by probe against test/fake-telegram.ts, which resolves chat refs numerically exactly as the real API does.
remediation: Canonicalize numerically, not textually: for a numeric ref return `BigInt(chat).toString()` (BigInt, so a supergroup id past 2^53 is not corrupted) rather than the raw string, so every spelling of one chat collapses to the single key inbound updates carry. Reject anything that does not round-trip.
testUpgrade: Widen the existing `SPELLINGS` table in test/inbound.test.ts (which today lists only already-canonical spellings) into a generator over EVERY textual spelling of one chat id — `-1009000001`, `-01009000001`, `-0000001009000001`, the same via chat_map, and the `@name` form — crossed with the existing FIRST_CALLS × arriveFirst axes, asserting post→fetchRecent round-trips and that the live subscriber sees the message. The class is 'two spellings of one chat must produce one key'; a table row per spelling makes any future ref format (a `+`-prefixed id, a huge supergroup id) fail independently.

summary: `poll_timeout_s` is accepted verbatim (`cfg.poll_timeout_s ?? 25`) with no range check, and the poll loop has no floor delay of its own. `0` — the value Telegram's own docs describe as 'short polling', and the value a reader of the README's 'latency/cost knob only' would naturally try — turns the single ingestion loop into an unthrottled request flood against the operator's bot token. A negative value silently kills ingestion outright.
failure: `connect({token, api_url, poll_timeout_s: 0})` issued 1545 `getUpdates` requests in one second (measured at the fake). Against real api.telegram.org that is an immediate flood-wait/ban on the operator's token. `poll_timeout_s: -5` produced 1 request in one second and then none: `pollBudgetMs()` goes negative, the AbortController fires before the request leaves, and the loop retries-and-aborts forever — live push and long-poll wakeups are dead for the process lifetime, with one throttled stderr line a minute as the only signal.
remediation: Validate at connect and fail fast: reject a `poll_timeout_s` outside `[1, 50]` (Telegram's accepted range) with an error naming the key, rather than accepting a value that either floods the vendor or disables the only ingestion path. Independently, give the poll loop a minimum inter-iteration delay so no configuration can spin it.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized `connect` config-validation table over every numeric knob (`poll_timeout_s`, `observed_retention_per_chat`, `observed_max_chats`) × every out-of-domain value (0, -1, 1.5, NaN, Infinity, 1e9), asserting connect REJECTS naming the key. Pair it with a loop-cadence invariant test — for any accepted `poll_timeout_s`, getUpdates calls in one second stay below a small constant — so the class 'a config value that turns the poll loop into a spin or a corpse' cannot come back through a different knob.
