summary: `readRetryAfter` caps Telegram's stated `retry_after` at 5s (`Math.min(header * 1000, 5000)`). net-util deliberately honours a server-stated wait IN FULL and documents why ('that is what escalates a rate limit into a ban'), and the sibling SaaS plugins comply — Discord's readRetryAfter says in so many words 'Return it UNCLAMPED', Zulip likewise. Telegram is the backend where this matters most: its flood-wait values are routinely 30s+, and retrying early extends them.
failure: A `sendMessage` 429 carrying `parameters.retry_after: 30` (a Telegram flood wait) is retried after 5000ms — 6x sooner than the vendor asked — up to 8 attempts, which is the documented path from a rate limit to a token ban. test/rate-limit.test.ts case 'body past the cap is capped' (retryAfterBody: 600 → expected 5000) cements the wrong behaviour as the contract.
remediation: Return the hint unclamped (`header * 1000`, else `parameters.retry_after * 1000`, else `undefined`) exactly as bridge-discord and bridge-zulip do, and let net-util's `clampBackoff` supply the default and `deadlineMs` refuse a wait that cannot fit. Update the rate-limit case to assert the full stated wait is honoured, or that the call ends rather than retrying early.
testUpgrade: Promote this to a shared, parameterized rate-limit-etiquette case run for every plugin that passes `retryAfterOf`: for stated waits of 1s/5s/30s/600s, assert the observed server-side gap is either >= the stated wait or the call rejects — never a retry sooner than stated. That guards the class ('a plugin re-implementing or re-tuning the shared backoff policy') across backends instead of pinning Telegram's 5s constant.

summary: The store's dedup check — the guarantee DESIGN §6, CLAUDE.md's v0.1 criterion and the README ('dedup across getUpdates backlog replays', 'the store's dedup makes that replay harmless') all name — is exercised by nothing. Deleting it leaves all 206 tests green. The fake deletes every update the client acknowledges via `offset`, so no test can re-deliver a consumed update, and no test calls `append` twice with the same composite id.
failure: Mutating `append`'s `if (this.seen.has(keyOf(observed))) return undefined;` to a no-op: `npx vitest run packages/bridge-telegram` → 206 passed, 1 skipped. A probe then showed the real consequence the suite cannot see — the same message re-delivered by getUpdates is pushed to a live subscriber twice as `[['-1009777001:4242','1','once'], ['-1009777001:4242','2','once']]`: one backendMsgId, two cursors, a direct DESIGN §6 violation.
remediation: Keep the check and cover it: add a fake capability to re-deliver an already-consumed update (the reason real Telegram re-serves a backlog when a poll's ack is lost), and a direct store-level case asserting `append` returns undefined for a repeat.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a 'same message observed twice' table over each ingest route — getUpdates replay of an unconfirmed update, a cold restart replaying the backlog, an own post whose sendMessage response is recorded and then also delivered, and two identical `store.append` calls — asserting in every cell that exactly one record exists, one live push fired, and fetchRecent returns it once. Guarding the ROUTE axis (not the one duplicate) is what keeps the class covered when a new ingest path is added.

summary: `call()` computes `pollBudgetMs()` and arms its own AbortController with it, but never forwards it to `fetchWithRetry` as `deadlineMs` — so net-util's `DEFAULT_DEADLINE_MS` (30 000) is the real ceiling. Since `pollBudgetMs()` exceeds 30 000 for any `poll_timeout_s` >= 22 (including the default 25), the plugin's own documented watchdog ('the long poll plus 40% slack') never governs, and at `poll_timeout_s` >= 30 every HEALTHY long poll is aborted mid-flight.
failure: `connect({..., poll_timeout_s: 35})`, then wait 32s with the fake parking the poll normally: stderr shows `parley-telegram: getUpdates failed, retrying: Telegram GET /getUpdates → deadline: no response within 30000ms`. Telegram accepts getUpdates timeouts up to 50s and most bot frameworks default to 30–50, so a documented 'latency/cost knob only' turns the sole ingestion path into a 30s abort-and-retry loop, whose diagnostic is throttled to one line a minute. The README's `subscribe` row credits this abandonment to a plugin watchdog that in fact never fires.
remediation: Pass `deadlineMs: budgetMs` through to `fetchWithRetry` alongside the local controller (or drop the local controller and rely solely on `deadlineMs`), so one number governs the call. Then the poll budget genuinely tracks `poll_timeout_s` instead of being silently overridden by the shared default.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the existing `telegram poll watchdog` describe — which only ever runs at `poll_timeout_s: 1`, below the crossover — over `poll_timeout_s` values that straddle net-util's default (1, 25, 35) and assert, for each, that a NORMALLY-answered long poll completes with no diagnostic AND that a `never-answer` stall is abandoned within ~`pollBudgetMs`. That guards the class 'a per-call budget the plugin computes but a shared helper overrides' for any future budget knob.

summary: `highWater()` is the entire boundary of `fetchRecent`'s loud 'cursor ahead of every message this store has observed' guard, and an off-by-one in it is invisible to the suite. Every cursor-lifecycle case uses damage that puts the held cursor two or more above the surviving high-water, so the one-record-lost case — the likeliest real corruption (a stale backup, a lost compaction rename) — is never exercised.
failure: Mutating `highWater()` to `return this.nextSeq;` → all 206 tests pass. A probe then reproduces the harm the suite misses: a store holding seqs 1..3 loses only its last line, the agent still holds cursor '3', and `fetchRecent({topic, since: '3'})` answers `{messages: [], nextCursor: '3'}` — a permanently short page, which the cursor-lifecycle suite's own docblock calls 'the one unacceptable answer' — instead of throwing.
remediation: Keep highWater as is and pin the boundary: add cursor-lifecycle cases where the damaged store's high-water sits exactly at, one below, and two below the held cursor, asserting serve / throw / throw respectively.
testUpgrade: Turn the `CASES` table in test/cursor-lifecycle.test.ts into a generator parameterized by `cursor - survivingHighWater ∈ {-1, 0, +1, +2}` (built by truncating the store file line-by-line rather than by hand-written damage functions), asserting 'serves everything after' for <= 0 and 'throws' for >= 1. That covers the CLASS of off-by-one in any store-versus-cursor staleness comparison, not one damage recipe.

summary: A `fetchRecent` with no `since` that is in flight when `disconnect()` runs resolves successfully with `nextCursor: '0'` instead of rejecting: the store reference was captured before the await, `close()` clears `byChat` so `maxSeq(chatId)` reads 0, and the plugin reports a topic tail of zero for a topic with history. The conformance suite's 'disconnect stops the plugin serving' case only ever exercises `post`.
failure: Three messages posted to `-1009123456` (real tail '3'); then `const p = plugin.fetchRecent({topic}); await plugin.disconnect(); await p` → `{messages: [], nextCursor: '0'}`. Core persists '0' as the topic's read position, so the next session's catch-up replays the entire retained window from the beginning — and the reported tail is simply false. Realistic on shutdown, when a `parley_fetch_recent` tool call is in flight as the bridge tears down.
remediation: Re-check liveness after every await in `fetchRecent` (and in `post` before `ingest`) and throw the 'not connected' error, rather than answering from a closed store; alternatively have `close()` preserve per-chat maxSeq. Never derive a cursor from a torn-down store.
testUpgrade: Add a parameterized teardown-race table to the conformance suite: for each seam call (`post`, `fetchRecent` with and without `since`, `fetchRecent` with `blockMs`, `subscribe`, `resolveIdentity`), issue it without awaiting, run `disconnect()` in the same turn, and assert the call either rejects or returns a cursor no lower than the caller's — never a fabricated tail. That guards the class 'a seam call resuming across teardown' for every backend.

summary: The plugin recovers HTTP statuses by regexing net-util's error prose (`/→ (\d{3})\b/`) even though net-util exports a typed `statusOf(err)` reading `HttpStatusError.status` — and net-util's JSDoc names this exact caller: 'a caller that branches on the status (Telegram's fatal getUpdates statuses) must use statusOf: recovering it by regex over prose makes any reword a silent behaviour change.' Telegram is the only plugin that branches on status, and it is the one ignoring the accessor, leaving net-util's `statusOf` with zero callers.
failure: Behaviourally equivalent today, but the failure mode is silent: reword `HttpStatusError`'s message (e.g. to `<label> (401): <body>`) and `statusOf` returns undefined, `?? 0` makes 401/403/404 non-fatal, and the poll loop retries a revoked token forever at 500ms instead of stopping loudly — the exact 'silent black hole hammering the API' the code comment says it prevents. `FATAL_POLL_STATUSES.includes(statusOf(err) ?? 0)` also treats an unparseable error as status 0, i.e. as retryable.
remediation: Import `statusOf` from `@sharptrick/parley-net-util` and delete the local regex copy; drop the `?? 0` in favour of an explicit undefined branch so an unclassifiable error is not silently reclassified as retryable.
testUpgrade: Add a shared net-util test asserting `statusOf` recovers the status from a thrown `HttpStatusError` for a table of statuses, plus a lint-style package test asserting no plugin src file contains a regex over `→` — the class is 'a plugin re-deriving structured data from a shared module's message prose', which will recur in any future error-shape branch.

summary: `ObservedStore` coerces a non-positive `maxPerChat`/`maxChats` to the built-in default (`maxPerChat > 0 ? maxPerChat : DEFAULT_MAX_PER_CHAT`). An operator who explicitly sets a retention bound to 0 or a negative number gets 10000/1000 instead — the opposite of what they asked for — with no error and no diagnostic, violating CLAUDE.md's fail-fast / no-silent-no-op rule on knobs the README presents as bounding history depth and disk use.
failure: `backend_config: { observed_retention_per_chat: 0, observed_max_chats: 0 }` yields a store retaining 10000 records across 1000 chats. An operator who set 0 believing it means 'keep nothing' (or who typo'd a negative) silently persists a deep local archive of every chat the bot is in, on disk, indefinitely — a privacy/disk surprise with no signal anywhere.
remediation: Reject a non-positive or non-integer bound at connect with an error naming the key, rather than substituting the default. If 'unbounded' or 'keep nothing' should be expressible, give them explicit spellings.
testUpgrade: Cover this in the same parameterized connect-config-validation table proposed for `poll_timeout_s`: every numeric knob × {0, -1, 1.5, NaN, Infinity} asserting connect rejects naming the key. One table guards the whole class of 'an out-of-domain knob value silently becomes the default'.

Better still, resolve every configured `chat_map` name during `connect` (already done) and document that only topics never named in `chat_map` pay a resolution on first use.

summary: `fetchWithRetry` documents (and its own comment insists) that a server-stated wait is honoured IN FULL because retrying sooner is what escalates a 429 into a ban — but the value used is `(await opts.retryAfterOf?.(res)) ?? retryAfterFromHeader(res)`, so a caller parser that returns a SMALLER number than the header wins outright. bridge-telegram and bridge-matrix both do exactly that (`Math.min(header * 1000, 5000)`), so the guarantee is false in production for two shipped backends.
failure: Upstream returns `429` with `Retry-After: 30` and the caller passes bridge-telegram's real `readRetryAfter`. Reproduced: `waits actually performed: [5000]` — the request is re-issued 25s earlier than Telegram asked, then repeats for up to 8 attempts. The module's entire stated safety property is silently overridden by the parser it delegates to.
remediation: Make the header a floor the caller cannot lower: `const header = retryAfterFromHeader(res); const parsed = await opts.retryAfterOf?.(res); const hinted = header === undefined ? parsed : Math.max(header, parsed ?? 0)`. Document `retryAfterOf` as "a source of an ADDITIONAL hint, never a ceiling", and drop the `Math.min(..., 5000)` clamps in bridge-telegram/bridge-matrix (the deadline is already the governor).
testUpgrade: Widen the existing 'never retries sooner than the server asked' table — which today only exercises the no-parser path — to a second dimension of `retryAfterOf` values per header row: `undefined`, `header/6` (a clamping parser), `header*2`, `0`, `NaN`, `-1`. Assert for every cell that every performed wait is >= the header's own delay-seconds/HTTP-date figure. That parameterization catches any future consumer parser that shrinks a stated wait, not just the two that do today.

summary: The `expect(activeTimers()).toBeLessThanOrEqual(timersBefore)` guard — written specifically because "a backoff timer left running past the rejection pins the event loop" — cannot fail. `timersBefore` is sampled AFTER `setTimeout(() => { stopped = true }, stopAtMs)` is armed and while vitest's own per-test timeout timer is live, so the baseline is inflated by timers that have expired or churned by the time of the comparison.
failure: Mutation: delete `cancels.push(() => clearInterval(poll))` from `sleepUnlessStopped` — 115/115 green. Delete `cancels.push(() => clearTimeout(waited))` as well, leaking BOTH a 25ms interval and a 5000ms timeout on every abandoned backoff — still 115/115 green. Sample the baseline before arming any test timer, and measure the delta of timers created by the module under test: wrap `setTimeout`/`setInterval`/`clearTimeout`/`clearInterval` in a counting proxy for the duration of the call and assert created === cleared. Alternatively assert on an exported handle count from the module rather than on `process.getActiveResourcesInfo()`.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a `timerLedger()` helper (created/cleared counts per timer kind) and apply it to EVERY case in this file that ends in a rejection or an early return — 429-exhaustion, deadline, stop-during-backoff, caller-abort, transport failure — asserting created === cleared for each. That covers the class 'a bounded wait leaks its timer on the abandonment path', which a single hand-written activeTimers() comparison in one row cannot.

summary: The suite's own self-tests pin only `cases().length > 10` and the single title 'topics are isolated'. Then a deleted or renamed case fails in this package rather than silently downgrading every backend's certification.

summary: No in-repo plugin other than the real backends is ever passed to `runConformanceSuite`, and the one obvious candidate — core's `FakePlugin`, whose docstring claims it "doubles as a sanity check that the conformance suite is backend-shaped, not SQLite-shaped" — demonstrably fails the suite. (2) 'disconnect is idempotent and stops the plugin serving': `post()` after `disconnect()` RESOLVES with '2' instead of rejecting — core's fake keeps serving writes after teardown, so every core test that uses it exercises semantics no conformant backend has.

summary: seam.ts's `fetchRecent` contract says a plugin that cannot represent an absent topic MAY throw `NoSuchTopicError`, and core has a whole module (no-such-topic.ts) mapping it to "topic not present yet". The suite's never-posted-topic case unconditionally requires an empty page, so a plugin exercising the documented alternative fails conformance — and no case anywhere exercises `NoSuchTopicError`, so core's mapping is never verified against a real plugin.

The suite certifies a contract narrower than the seam it claims to be written against.
remediation: Either narrow seam.ts (drop the MAY, requiring an empty replayable page — then core's NoSuchTopicError path is dead for `fetchRecent`) or teach the suite both arms: accept an empty page OR a rejection that `instanceof`/`name`-matches NoSuchTopicError, and add a positive case asserting the error's shape (name, `topic` field) so core's mapping has a producer.
testUpgrade: A parameterized 'absent topic' case over both permitted outcomes, driven by a new required context field (e.g. `absentTopicBehaviour: 'empty-page' | 'throws'`) so a backend must state which it implements and cannot omit it — plus a broken-variant fixture that throws a plain Error for an absent topic and must fail. Guards the class 'the suite pins one arm of a MAY in the seam'.

summary: `redactUrls` has two halves — an exact `split(url)` and the `URL_LIKE` regex sweep — and only the first is ever exercised. All four rows of the 'never leaks a credential-bearing URL' table produce error text containing the request URL byte-for-byte, so the regex, which is the half that catches a URL the transport spelled differently, is dead weight in the test suite and can be removed silently.
failure: Mutation: `return text.split(url).join('<url>');` (regex sweep deleted) — 129/129 green, including every credential-leak row. The realistic case it guards is untested: a proxy/undici message that normalizes the URL (`https://api.example.test:443/bot123:TOKEN/getMe`, a trailing slash, percent-encoding differences, a redirect target) is not a substring of the caller's URL, so with the regex gone the bot token reaches the thrown message → the MCP `isError` result → model context and operator logs.

Also consider that `URL_LIKE` is scheme-anchored, so a body echoing only the credential-bearing PATH still leaks — redact the token-shaped path segments too, or state the limit in the README.

Assert the canary is absent in every cell. That covers the class 'redaction only catches the exact spelling' rather than the one spelling tried.

summary: 'never skips a case on a self-declared capability flag' greps only for `testCtx.skip()`. A case that silently early-`return`s on a capability flag — the cheapest and most likely way to reintroduce exactly the coverage-for-a-boolean trade the guard exists to prevent — is invisible to it, as are `it.skip`, `describe.skip`, `it.skipIf` and `this.skip()`.

Apply it to all cases, not to a title allowlist.

summary: `statusOf` and `HttpStatusError.status` exist precisely so a caller never re-parses the message ("recovering it by regex over prose makes any reword a silent behaviour change"), and the README says "Branch on this instead of re-parsing the message". The only consumer in the repo that branches on status, bridge-telegram, defines its own shadowing `statusOf` at index.ts:753 that regexes `/→ (\d{3})\b/` out of the message. Nothing enforces the seam it advertises.
failure: bridge-telegram's poll loop treats 401/403/404 as fatal. Its regex takes the FIRST `→ NNN` in the message, and the transport/deadline envelopes (`L → transport: <sanitized untrusted body>`) contain no status — so an upstream error body containing the text `→ 403` makes Telegram classify a transient transport failure as a fatal auth error and abandon `getUpdates` permanently. Also, the terminal 429-exhaustion rejection is a plain Error, so `statusOf` returns undefined for the one status this module is built around.
remediation: Have bridge-telegram import `statusOf` from this package and delete its local copy; make the terminal 429 rejection an `HttpStatusError` (or a sibling class carrying `status: 429`) so `statusOf` is total over status failures; and keep untrusted body text out of any prefix a caller might parse.
testUpgrade: A repo-graph test in this package (it already reads sibling manifests for the consumer-set assertions): for every package depending on `@sharptrick/parley-net-util`, assert its sources contain no `→\s*\(?\\d{3}` style regex over an error message, and that any local function named `statusOf` is an import. Plus a parameterized case asserting `statusOf(err) === 429` after 429-exhaustion, and that a hostile body containing `→ 401` cannot change any caller's classification.

summary: Every case posts short ASCII ('a', 'same', 'm0', 'x for @second-writer'). The suite never certifies that `post` round-trips content at all faithfully — no newlines, no leading/trailing whitespace, no non-BMP/emoji, no empty string, and no length near a backend's cap. So the same `parley_post` behaves four different ways across certified backends.
failure: A 3000-character post: bridge-discord throws a specific, helpful error at `CONTENT_LIMIT = 2000` (index.ts:265); bridge-telegram has no guard at all and forwards it, so the user gets a raw `Telegram POST /sendMessage → 400: …` envelope at Telegram's 4096 cap; nothing in the shared suite distinguishes these, and a backend that silently TRUNCATED to its cap would be certified conformant while losing user data.
remediation: Add a content-fidelity case to the suite: post a payload containing a newline, leading/trailing spaces, an emoji and a combining sequence, and assert `fetchRecent` returns it byte-identical (or that the plugin rejects it, never silently alters it). Add a declared `maxContentChars` capability to ConformanceContext and assert `post` at the cap round-trips and above the cap rejects with a message naming the limit — which is also the seam's missing documented answer to "how long may content be".
testUpgrade: Parameterized fidelity table: `it.each([['newline','a\nb'],['crlf','a\r\nb'],['leading space',' a'],['emoji','a😀b'],['combining','é vs é'],['at-cap','X'.repeat(ctx.maxContentChars)],['over-cap','X'.repeat(ctx.maxContentChars+1)]])`, asserting exact round-trip or a rejection that names the limit — never silent alteration. Guards the class 'content is mutated or dropped by a certified backend' for payload shapes nobody has tried yet.

summary: `NEUTRALIZED` covers C0, DEL, U+2028/2029 and bidi controls but not the C1 range U+0080–U+009F. U+0085 (NEL) is a line terminator in most terminals and in several log pipelines, and U+009B (CSI) is the 8-bit form of an ANSI escape introducer — both are exactly the "forge line structure" capability the docstring says it removes.
failure: `sanitizeBody('line1line2more')` returns the string unchanged (verified against the character class). A hostile backend returning that as a 500 body gets a forged extra line in the operator's stderr and in the model-visible `isError` result, past a guard documented as flattening body structure.
remediation: Extend the class to `-` (and consider U+FEFF/U+180E). Also slice on code points rather than UTF-16 units so truncation cannot emit a lone surrogate into an MCP JSON result.
testUpgrade: Replace the hand-listed sanitizeBody table with a generator over categories: all of C0, all of C1, DEL, U+2028/2029, U+200E/200F, U+202A-202E, U+2066-2069, plus a lone-surrogate and an astral char at the truncation boundary — asserting the output contains no character in `\p{Cc}\p{Cf}` other than the ones deliberately allowed, and that its length never grows. That guards the class 'a control-character family was omitted' instead of the six characters someone thought of.

summary: `sleepUnlessStopped` contains `if (settled !== undefined) { clearTimeout(waited); return settled; }` immediately after `setTimeout(...)`. No real runtime fires a timer synchronously, so that branch is unreachable in production; it exists solely because the tests' `captureWaits()` replaces global `setTimeout` with a function that invokes its callback inline. A shipped module carries a defensive branch for a behaviour only its own fake exhibits, and the fake means every wait-related assertion measures a recorded number rather than an elapsed wait.

remediation: Inject the timer instead of stubbing the global: add an optional `sleep`/`scheduler` seam (or reuse the existing `now` injection point) so tests can observe requested waits without making time synchronous, then delete the branch. Alternatively assign `resolveWait` before arming any timer so the ordering hazard cannot exist at all.
testUpgrade: Convert the wait assertions to a fake clock that advances explicitly (vi.useFakeTimers + advanceTimersByTimeAsync, or an injected scheduler recording (ms, resolve) pairs) rather than a synchronous setTimeout, and add a case asserting `sleepUnlessStopped` resolves when the timer fires on a LATER macrotask. Guards the class 'a test double whose semantics no runtime has, forcing a branch into shipped code'.

summary: 'documents the required field `%s`' is `expect(readme).toContain(field)`. For `plugin` the README's prose ("run it against every backend plugin") satisfies it, so the field could be undocumented — or the entire ConformanceContext code block deleted — and the row still passes. The same weakness applies to net-util's `it.each(Object.keys(api))('documents the exported `%s`')`, where short names like `delay` match incidental prose.

remediation: Assert inside the extracted code fence, not over the whole file: pull the ```ts block containing `interface ConformanceContext`, and require each field to appear there as a declaration (`^\s*field[?]?:`). Same for net-util: require each export name inside a bullet/backticked context.

Guards the class 'toContain over a whole doc counts prose as documentation'.

summary: `isAccessToken` returns false for ANY JWT carrying a `nonce` claim. No specification forbids `nonce` in an access token (RFC 9068 does not), and several IdPs mint it there — Keycloak did so for auth-code flows until it was moved to the ID token only in v25, and the README markets this mode for "Keycloak (or any spec-compliant OIDC provider)".
failure: Against such an IdP, every token from an authorization-code flow that carried a nonce is rejected with the deliberately opaque `invalid or expired access token`. The connector sees a permanent 401 loop with no server-side signal distinguishing it from a bad audience mapper or a clock problem — and the shipped keycloak.e2e.test.ts uses the password grant, which never carries a nonce, so the e2e gate cannot see it either. Not reproduced against a real pre-25 realm; the code path is traced and the claim in the doc-comment ("an IdP that does not stamp `typ` still gives an ID token away this way") is what I am contesting.
remediation: Rely on the `typ` allowlist/denylist, which is normative for the IdPs actually named, and demote the nonce heuristic to a rejection only when no `typ` is present anywhere AND an ID-token-only claim such as `at_hash`/`auth_time` also appears — or make it opt-out via config. Either way, log the discriminating reason server-side while keeping the client-facing message opaque.
testUpgrade: Widen the TOKEN_KINDS table in oidc-token-kinds.test.ts from (claims, header) pairs to a matrix over {typ absent / Bearer / ID / Refresh} x {nonce absent / present} x {at_hash absent / present}, with the expected verdict stated per cell. That forces the question "which combination actually identifies an ID token" to be answered explicitly and makes any future tightening or loosening of the heuristic a visible table edit.

summary: The cursor deliberately carries the store's identity (`<storeId>.<rowid>`) so a recreated file cannot be mistaken for the old one, but backendMsgId is the bare rowid. Core dedups on backendMsgId in a per-process, per-topic SeenSet of 4096 ids, so after a store reset within one process's lifetime the new store's ids 1..N collide with the old store's and the replayed messages are dropped as duplicates — the exact failure the storeId prefix was added to prevent, on the other half of the §6 contract.
failure: Store reset while a bridge process lives: old store's ids '1'..'20' are in SeenSet['ctx'] from catch-up; the file is recreated (or db_path is repointed); the new store's first 20 messages also mint backendMsgId '1'..'20' and core's SeenSet.markSeen/has drops every one — silent message loss, invisible in the plugin's own tests because packages/bridge-sqlite/test/cursor-replay.test.ts's 'catch-up across a real store reset loses nothing' asserts only the plugin's returned contents, never core's dedup verdict. Marked PLAUSIBLE rather than CONFIRMED because the only in-process route to a reset is a second connect(), which is itself broken (see the reconnect finding), so today the collision is reached only via that path.
remediation: Qualify the dedup key the same way the cursor is qualified — return `asBackendMsgId(`${storeId}.${rowid}`)` from post() and rowToMessage() — so the two halves of the §6 contract share one identity namespace. If the bare rowid must stay for compatibility, state in the README that backendMsgId is only unique within one store generation and that read-state AND the seen-set must be discarded together on a reset.
testUpgrade: Add a cursor/dedup-identity table to test/cursor-replay.test.ts that runs the reset scenarios through core's SeenSet + catchUpTopic rather than through the plugin alone, guarding the CLASS 'two messages that are distinct under the cursor are distinct under the dedup key': for each of [same store, store reset, restore-from-backup, foreign-store cursor] assert that catchUpTopic reports the full expected message count with a SeenSet carried across the boundary. Parameterize by generation count so a future backend meeting the same theme (Redis stream recreate, Telegram store reset) can reuse it.

summary: buildSchema() unconditionally emits `DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS ...; CREATE TRIGGER ...` and connect() runs it on every start, even when the schema is already correct. Both statements take an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the shared message table, so every process start blocks all posts and all reads from every other bridge process sharing the database - the deployment shape README lines 67-77 explicitly recommends.
failure: N bridge processes share one table; a supervisor restarts them (rolling deploy, crash loop, config reload). Each restart's bootstrap transaction takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the message table, serializing every in-flight post() and fetchRecent() cluster-wide for the duration of the DDL; a restart storm turns that into repeated stalls. The advisory lock at index.ts:247 serializes bootstraps against each other but not against posts. Marked PLAUSIBLE: traced from the statement text and PostgreSQL's documented lock levels, not reproduced under load - nothing in the suite ever runs connect() concurrently with another instance's traffic.
remediation: Make the trigger DDL conditional: skip the DROP/CREATE when a trigger of that name already exists on that relation (a pg_trigger lookup inside the same advisory-locked transaction), or use PostgreSQL 14+'s CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER and issue it only when the existing definition differs. The advisory lock stays; the table-level lock becomes a first-bootstrap cost instead of a per-connect one.
testUpgrade: Add a real-server case class 'connect() on an already-bootstrapped table does not block a concurrent writer', parameterized over {fresh table, already-bootstrapped table} x {1, 4 concurrent posters}: hold a steady post loop from one plugin, connect a second, and assert the poster's worst-case latency on the already-bootstrapped arm stays within a small multiple of its baseline. That also pins the general class 'connect() is cheap and non-disruptive when there is nothing to create'.

summary: `room_preset` accepts `trusted_private_chat`, which the README's config table and its "topic rooms are invite-only" section never mention. Per the Matrix spec that preset gives every invitee the room creator's power level (100), so any invited peer can change `m.room.join_rules` to public, kick the bridge, or invite strangers — defeating the invite-only guarantee the section promises.
failure: `backend_config: { room_preset: 'trusted_private_chat', invite: ['@peer:host'] }` reads as "a more trusted private room" from the type alone; the created room's join rule is `invite`, so the provisioning test's `expect(preset).not.toBe('public_chat')` passes, yet `@peer` can immediately set join_rule to `public` and open the topic's history and its `<channel>` injection surface to the whole federation.
remediation: Either drop `trusted_private_chat` from the accepted union (nothing in the package uses it) or document it in the README config table with the power-level consequence spelled out next to the invite-only promise.
testUpgrade: CLASS: every value a config union accepts is documented and graded. Drive the provisioning table over ALL members of the `room_preset` union (not just the default and `public_chat`), and add a README-vs-code check — a test that reads the union's members out of the source and asserts each appears in packages/bridge-matrix/README.md's config table, the same shape the cursor-form SHAPES table uses to keep the README diffable.

summary: The README's catch-up guidance ("Configure a **large `catchup.limit`** for Slack: the aggregate cost falls linearly with it") and the plugin's hard-coded `limit: 200` per history page both assume the classic tiered allowance for `conversations.history`. Slack materially tightened that method for apps not distributed on the Marketplace (widely reported as roughly 1 request/minute with a ~15-object page cap). If that applies, `limit: 200` is silently truncated by the server, the documented `backlog²/(2·limit·page)` cost model is off by more than an order of magnitude, and "configure a large `catchup.limit`" is the wrong advice — a backlog drain becomes effectively impossible rather than merely slow.
failure: Not reproducible against the in-process fake, which mirrors the shape (`response_metadata.next_cursor`, newest-first, exclusive `oldest`) but not the vendor's allowance: `FakeSlack.PAGE_SIZE = 50` and no rate limiting at all. `src/index.ts:333` sends `limit: 200` unconditionally; nothing in the suite would notice a server that returns 15. A real workspace on the newer tier: `fetchRecent({since})` over a 10k-message backlog needs ~670 requests at ~1/min — hours per call, versus the README's stated "real wall-clock time".
remediation: Verify the current `conversations.history` tier and page cap against Slack's live rate-limit docs (per CLAUDE.md's gate discipline, the docs win). Then either derive the page `limit` from config with a documented default matching the tier, or state the tier and its consequence explicitly in the *Catch-up cost* paragraph, and reconcile the `catchup.limit` advice with the real page cap. Add the tier to the provisioning section alongside the scope table.

summary: On the resume-after-`since` path the walk must reach the oldest end before it can publish a safe `nextCursor`, so exceeding `MAX_HISTORY_PAGES` throws. Because the cursor cannot advance, the throw repeats on every subsequent catch-up: a topic whose backlog above the stored cursor exceeds 2000 pages is wedged permanently with no in-band recovery.
failure: A channel accumulating more than MAX_HISTORY_PAGES × page messages above the stored cursor (400k at the current 200/page; ~30k if the server caps pages at 15 — see the tier finding) makes `fetchRecent({since})` reject with `exceeded 2000 pages` on every call, forever. `catchUpTopic` propagates it (only `NoSuchTopicError` is absorbed), so catch-up for that topic never runs again and the only fix is hand-editing the read-state file. `http-contract.test.ts` proves the walk *terminates*; nothing tests that the bridge can ever make progress again afterwards.
remediation: Make the cap recoverable instead of terminal: bound each window with `latest` in addition to `oldest` (Slack supports both) so a page-capped walk can still return a correct oldest-first window and a `nextCursor` that sits below nothing unread. Failing that, surface the condition as a distinguishable error type and document the operator recovery step (reset the topic's cursor) in the README next to the *Bounded waits* paragraph.
testUpgrade: Extend the `PAGERS` table with a RECOVERY dimension: after a row hits its termination guard, re-run `fetchRecent` with the same `since` against a now-smaller backlog and assert the call makes progress. Parameterize over cap-shape {repeated cursor, fresh-cursor-forever, page count just over MAX_HISTORY_PAGES} so "terminates" and "can still catch up" are both graded.

summary: `reconnect()`'s catch does `this.wsReady = undefined; // clear the rejected attempt so the next loop retries`, but `ensureSocket`'s own rejection handler already does it, and correctly — guarded by `if (this.wsReady === attempt)`. The unguarded copy in `reconnect` is dead in the common path and actively wrong if a newer attempt has been memoized in between: it discards a live, in-flight handshake.
failure: If any caller reaches `ensureSocket()` between `ensureSocket`'s rejection handler and `reconnect`'s catch (both microtasks on the same rejection), `wsReady` holds a fresh attempt B when `reconnect` blanks it. The next `ensureSocket()` then starts attempt C concurrently with B; `openSocket` overwrites `this.ws`, so B's socket is orphaned — nothing ever closes it (its close handler short-circuits on `this.ws !== ws`), consuming one of the ~10 Socket Mode connections per app token. Narrow window, but the line buys nothing and the comment asserts a job the other site already owns.
remediation: Delete the line and its comment; `ensureSocket`'s identity-guarded invalidation is the single owner of that field. If a guard is wanted here it must carry the same identity check.
